p: The air in the Wandering Glade hummed with ancient magic as Drake stood beside the silver water, his legs still unsteady. The Stream's visions lingered like afterimages behind his eyes—a truth both exhilarating and terrifying.
Cassian's hand remained firm on his arm, an anchor in the aftermath. Lyra wiped tears from her glowing eyes while Echo kept her daggers ready, scanning the glade for threats.

The elves watched wordlessly, their silver eyes unreadable. Their leader, the eldest Keeper, Lyran, stepped forward, his hair once the color of midnight now streaked with blue, a half-veil of silver shimmering across his ancient eyes.

"What you have experienced, young Drakkyn, few have survived with their minds intact," Lyran said, his voice a melodic whisper that seemed to resonate with the very current of the Silver Stream. "The Stream shows not what we wish to see, but what we need to understand."
Drake found his voice at last. "Those weren't just my memories. I saw... others. Ancient ones."
"The blood remembers," Lyran said simply. "Even when the mind forgets." He studied Drake with newfound interest. "You seek the Shadow's Edge—a fragment of power older than any kingdom of man or elf."
Cassian stepped forward. "We come on behalf of—"
"Queen Titania, yes," Lyran interrupted, a hint of amusement in his voice. "Her messengers reached us before you did. But royal seals and urgent pleas do not change our duty as Keepers."
Echo's patience visibly thinned. "Then what does? Because while we stand here exchanging pleasantries, the rift grows. We've seen what comes through."
"And you believe this fragment will seal it?" Lyran asked.
"We know it will," Cassian said firmly. "The Scythe was forged to help bind realms together. Its fracturing is what allowed the breach to form, unchecked, in the first place."
Lyran exchanged glances with the other elves. A silent communication seemed to pass between them before he turned back to the group.

"For centuries, we have guarded this place, not because we were ordered to, but because we understand what would happen if its power fell into the wrong hands." His gaze settled on Drake. "But the Stream has made its choice. It recognized something in you—something beyond your Drakkyn heritage."
Drake felt a chill run down his spine. "What do you mean?"

"The Stream does not show its memories to everyone who touches it. Most see only reflections of themselves, nothing more. You saw beyond—into lives not your own, into the very history of your kind." Lyran's expression softened slightly. "That is rare, even among the ancient bloodlines."
Lyra stepped closer to Drake, her staff glowing faintly. "Does that mean ye'll help us?"
Lyran smiled, showing teeth white as snow. "This remains to be seen my dear…”
He gestured, and the surface of the stream roiled, a pale vortex opening at its center. From its depths, something glowed, limned with ghostly violet light.
Before the party could approach, the air shifted—like a curtain being yanked aside. A laugh, high and clear, echoed through the clearing.
"Well, isn't this touching," came a voice, soft but edged with mischief. "But surely you don't mean to conclude the ritual without a proper audience?"

From the shadows at the far end of the clearing stepped a lean figure with a fox's grin and eyes that glittered like stars. His russet hair tangled wildly, and tiny bells on his cuffs rang cheerfully.
Lyran's eyes narrowed. "Robin Goodfellow," he said, the name sharp with displeasure. "Your presence was not requested."

Robin bowed with exaggerated elegance. "And yet, at your service, as ever, Lyran. Though I must say, your hospitality has waned over the centuries." His words carried a musical lilt, almost dancing between them. "Such serious expressions on such a magnificent night! When the moons are high and magic flows like wine."
He moved to the edge of the vortex and smiled at Drake, his voice shifting to a more rhythmic cadence:
"Dragon-child, with eyes so bright,
You peer beyond the mortal sight.
But do you see the patterns true,
Or just the spaces shining through?"
Drake felt strangely drawn to Robin—something about him reminded Drake of stories his mother had read, then it dawned on him. "You're the trickster. The Puck. From the older plays and stories."

Robin's eyes lit up. "Oh, well done! The mortal world hasn't forgotten everything of value, I see." He circled Drake with curious interest. "But tell me, Drake Veridian, does your world's Puck ever ask for payment in truth? Because here, the price is always truth, and sometimes the coin weighs heavier than expected."
Lyra stepped back. "Ye cannae trust a wyld fae, they are mischievous by nature." she muttered, though she seemed just as captivated as the rest.

Robin sauntered to the center of the peninsula and faced Lyran. "The Stream has made its choice, old friend. Even you must acknowledge its wisdom." His voice carried authority beneath its playfulness.
Lyran nodded, acknowledging the truth of Robin's words. "The Shadow's Edge is theirs, as the Stream has decreed."
Robin gestured for Drake to approach the swirling heart of the stream. "Go on, then. What waits has waited long enough."
Drake stepped forward, drawn by both Robin's strange magnetism and the importance of the quest. He reached into the water, the cold so intense it burned.

His hand closed around something solid—a shard of black metal covered in a Noachian script that shimmered in the moonlight. As he held the Shadow's Edge for the first time, it was like all the shadows around the glade seemed to shift, and stretch as if being drawn toward Drake and the fragment.
Robin clapped, his voice rising at this crucial moment:
"Well done, brave heart, the prize is won!
But heed this warning ere you're done:
What you now hold with trembling hand
May weigh much more than you had planned."
Drake stumbled back, piece in hand, suddenly lightheaded. Cassian steadied him while Echo watched Robin and the elves with wary eyes.
Lyran's voice softened with something like regret. "Take it, and go. But remember: the scythe's hunger is never satisfied for long."

Robin bounced through the glade like a living spark, drawing every eye as he wove between moonbeams and shadow. "Ready for a woodland stroll, heroes? Or would you rather camp here and hope the trees don't get hungry?" His eyes twinkled with mischief.
Echo glanced at Drake. "Do we have to follow him?" she whispered. "I'd sooner trust a rabid hedgehog."
Drake shrugged, still feeling the fragment's pulse against his skin. "He got us this far. And I think he wants us to succeed."

The group followed Robin through the Eldrinwood, where he led them not by path or landmark, but by whim. Sometimes he vanished entirely, leaving only laughter to guide them. Once, he stopped to play a game with sprites, betting his own shadow—which he lost, then regained by dusk.
In one clearing, Cassian fell behind. Drake matched his pace. "You okay?" Drake asked quietly.

Cassian looked up. "When I saw you in the stream, I thought for a moment you'd be lost. I don't know if I could have pulled you out." He paused. "I mean, not that I would have wanted to, or anything."
Drake's heart quickened. "I don't think you can lose me that easily," he said.

Robin appeared beside them, his voice gentle but knowing. "The heart speaks truest in the wild places, doesn't it? Where masks slip and walls crumble." Then, with a more serious tone: "Keep an eye on that fragment, dragon-boy. Sometimes sharp things cut both ways."

Eventually, the trees thinned. Robin stopped and bowed theatrically. "Here ends my tour. If you want to find the dwarves, head north. You'll smell the fire before you see the smoke." He winked at Echo, who responded with a rude gesture.
Lyra lingered. "Will we see ye again?" she asked.
Robin grinned, bright and wild, his words flowing into rhythm once more:
"When tales need spice and plots need twist,
When paths grow dark and hope is missed,
Look for me then—or don't at all—
I come when stories rise, and fall!"
He produced a silver flower from nowhere, tucked it into Lyra's hair, and vanished.

The party stood at the forest's edge, four souls with more scars and fewer illusions than when they entered. They set off toward the dwarves, the scythe fragment secure in Drake's pack and Robin's laughter still echoing somewhere in the night.
Behind them, the Silver Stream continued its silent, endless course, carrying all their stories into whatever tomorrow waited beyond the trees..

ch.src: Sebastian Nightwell and Thaddeus Johnson, Heart of the Drakkyn (2025), Chapter 20
p: Thunder pealed through the black Louisiana sky, rattling the warped glass in the windows of Celestine Loa's moss-choked hut. The eaves shuddered as rain pelted the palm-thatched roof in waves, swelling and breaking like a fever. Inside, blue candles guttered in half-empty jars—rowed along the base of a makeshift cradle, their flames hunched low, trembling before each fresh boom from above.

The air was thick with the tang of wet earth and a sharper, resinous note from the herbs smoldering in the fireplace. Over the hush of storm and the fretful hiss of wind in the cypress, a midwife's voice rasped through a string of ancient syllables, each sound clipped, urgent, shaped by a tongue that had worked this litany a thousand times before.

Celestine knelt on the packed dirt floor, thighs slick with sweat and afterbirth, fingers sunk white-knuckled into the tattered edge of her own cotton shift. Every pain was sharp and clean, a promise. The midwife's hands were sure, practiced, she knew, down to the root, that this birth was different.

A final spasm—white-hot, dazzling, ripping her open—and the room seemed to freeze on a held breath. Then, in the blue-and-shadow flicker, a new sound: a baby's thin, raw howl, startling and pure, slicing through the moment like a thrown blade.

The child was slippery and long-limbed, flecked with blood and amniotic sheen, but already her lungs were strong—every cry a small storm of its own. The midwife wrapped her in a rough flannel, then held her up for Celestine's inspection: a daughter, hair already dark, skin gold even in the gloom.
The hut stilled. The old woman's chant collapsed to a hush. Even the wind hesitated, as if the world wanted to hear what came next.

Celestine reached with trembling hands, but not for the baby, not yet. She pointed, first, to the potted fern in the window-ledge. It sat tangled in its own roots, a huddle of green snaking through a clay pot caked with dust and dried salt. As the child's second wail split the air, the fern shuddered; its curled tips unfurled in slow, deliberate sequence, leaf after leaf extending as though saluting a sovereign.
The midwife's eyes grew round and white. "She bringin' the green awake," she breathed, voice hoarse with awe. "She bringin' the storm, too."
Celestine only grinned, the split in her lower lip weeping fresh blood. "Let it come," she whispered. "Ain't never been a Loa afraid of a little rain."
A silence rode the next few seconds. Out in the night, the barnyard hens—

usually such nervous, gossiping creatures—had gone completely mute. Not a cluck, not a scratch or peck, just the tense, uncertain hush of animals who sensed the boundary between worlds had been disturbed.

The newborn's cry diminished into a throaty, grumbling coo. The midwife bent close, peering into the infant's face. "Those eyes," she muttered, and crossed herself in two quick strokes. "Ain't right for a baby to come out looking that old."

It was true. The child's eyes, still gummy with vernix and barely open, were a depthless brown—so dark they seemed black in the candlelight, and so unblinking they seemed to trap and hold every flicker and shift of the flame. There was a patience in them that wasn't learned but born, as if this girl were already tired of the world, already weighing it and finding it wanting.
The midwife shuddered and set the child gently into the cradle, then wiped her hands on her apron and backed away, whispering another string of protection prayers.

Celestine was slow to rise, but she did. Her own arms were marked with shallow cuts—ritual, not accident. She moved to the cradle, candles painting her shadow in wild loops along the water-stained walls.
The storm broke again—thunder rolling so close it seemed to split the roof in two. The blue flames ducked low, and for a heartbeat all was pitch, nothing but the scent of newborn and herbs.

She leaned in, close enough to see her own face reflected in the child's glassy stare. She studied it—the line of the jaw, the fragile slant of nose, the knotted little hands. Then, reverently, she brushed one fingertip across the baby's damp brow.

She did not bother with the usual words: not the names of saints or the hopeful naming of future husbands, not the soft lies about happiness or safety. Instead, Celestine let her lips curve into a smile that was equal parts pride, mischief, and challenge.
"Welcome, Zariah," she murmured, voice thick and sweet as chicory. "Let's see what you do with the world, little queen."
Outside, the hens began to mutter again, uneasy but drawn to the light in the hut. The storm lingered, but with every flicker of the blue candle, it receded—
until what remained was just the rain, and the sound of a girl's first night on earth, already claimed by thunder.

By the time Zariah was old enough to walk, the storm outside was an afterthought; the real weather was inside, where her mother's parlor was thick with the musty perfume of roots and rain-damp leaves. Walls, crowded tight with darkened shelves, sagged beneath rows of glass jars, each one packed and labeled in Celestine's slanting, precise hand: Angelica Root, Blue Flag Iris, Devil's Claw, Sunflower Seeds black as midnight, and Cowrie Shells white as Kaolin. The few windows admitted only a muddy, green-tinted daylight, so that everything was lit by a smoky lantern suspended from the ceiling, its glow turning the dust into slow-moving gold.

"Pay attention, Zari," Celestine intoned, nudging the child's elbow with the blunt back of a spoon. "If you add too much, the tea will taste like coffin-wood, and you don't want to be known for that."

Zariah leaned in, nose nearly pressed to the rim of the stoneware bowl. She was five, and already her fingers were deft enough to measure bitter powder to the quarter-pinch. She slid a thin slice of bark into the bowl and watched it swirl in the pale syrup of sugar and water, the grains clumping into small, slow clouds before dissolving.

Celestine's hands were callused, hard from years in the garden and at the stove, but her touch on Zariah's shoulder was always gentle. "Now you stir," she said. "Seven times, widdershins." Zariah stirred, careful to keep her turns even and her face blank. The taste of the powder on her tongue was sharp and electric; she wanted to spit, but knew better.
"Good. Now, say it."

Zariah closed her eyes and recited, as she'd been taught, the invocation to the river Loa—low and melodic, the words stitched with consonants that curled and snapped like brambles. Celestine watched, arms folded, as her daughter completed the litany, never missing a syllable or a beat.

When Zariah was finished, she looked up, waiting. Celestine nodded once, then poured the mixture into a fat-bellied glass jar, which she set on the sill next to the potted fern. "That's for the water spirits," she said, with a glance toward the slow-moving river out back. "They like their offerings sweet, but not too sweet. Like men."
Zariah giggled, then snatched the empty bowl and licked the edge, careful not to waste a drop.

This was the rhythm of her days: sunrise with Celestine in the garden, midmorning in the parlor learning the properties of every root and bark, afternoons lost in the trance of mortar and pestle or in the careful tracing of chalk symbols on the floor. When her mother's customers visited, Zariah hovered at the edge of the room, listening to every complaint and diagnosis, memorizing the way Celestine's hands moved—fast and secretive when mixing a charm, slow and deliberate when smoothing a poultice onto someone's fevered brow.

At dusk, Zariah practiced sigils on the bare earth behind the hut, using river mud or ground-up chalk. She drew them in concentric circles, each more complex than the last, and recited their meanings in a whisper, as if she was afraid the air might steal them.
"Your hands are too clean," Celestine told her once, with a smile. "No good Mambo ever kept her hands clean. Not even the saints."
Zariah took this as a challenge, and the next week she was black to the elbows with clay and pigment, nails rimmed with green.

By the time she was seven, there was no plant in the garden whose name she didn't know, no charm in her mother's arsenal she hadn't committed to memory. She learned fast, and she learned with a hunger that was obvious to anyone who visited.
On the morning of her seventh birthday, Celestine woke Zariah before dawn. "Up, girl," she said. "There's work to do, and you got an audience."

They stepped outside into a world painted grey and silver. The grass sparkled, wet with dew, and the air was already thickening with the day's heat. Celestine set a basket of rose petals and another of smooth river stones on the ground, and together they marked out a circle behind the hut, Zariah spacing the petals with a methodical precision that would have made her ancestors proud.

Inside the circle, Zariah drew a sigil—one she'd never been allowed to practice before, not even in mud. It was complex, composed of curves and hooked angles that demanded steady hands. She finished it in three careful passes, then stood back, waiting.

Celestine stepped into the house and returned with two visitors: one old man, stooped and gnarled as a cypress root, and a woman with hair braided so tight it shone like wet rope. They sat on stools at the edge of the circle, saying nothing, just watching.
"Ready?" Celestine asked.
Zariah nodded, throat dry.
Celestine raised a brow. "Then begin."

The ritual was short but exacting. Zariah traced the sigil's lines with the tip of her right index finger, reciting the names of the river Simbi in a steady, rising chant. She felt the words thrumming in her belly, a vibration that grew stronger with each repetition. At the final syllable, she slapped her palm flat onto the earth and let the last of the air in her lungs out in a rush.
Nothing happened at first. For a long moment, the world was just the hush of dawn and the scent of rose petals and the old man's steady, wheezing breath.

Then, from the center of the sigil, a faint white vapor began to curl. It snaked upward, twisting around itself, coiling and uncoiling like a serpent made of fog and memory. The snake hovered above the ground, then darted in a brief, intricate dance around Zariah's ankles before vanishing with a sound like a single, plucked violin string.
The old woman let out a low, approving hum. The man just smiled, teeth white and shining in the dark slot of his mouth.

Celestine moved forward and pressed her thumb to Zariah's forehead, leaving a print of pale ash. "That's my girl," she said, pride burning in her eyes. "Seven years old, and you've called a Simbi to you. Not even your granny did it that young."
Zariah beamed, shoulders squaring, feet solid in the earth. She barely heard the polite clapping of the elders, so full was she with the bright, terrifying thrill of success.
That night, when Celestine tucked her in and smoothed her hair, Zariah asked, "Mama, what did the spirits say?"
Celestine kissed her brow, lips lingering just a little longer than usual. "They said you got old blood in you, Zari. Old as the river itself."
Zariah fell asleep to the song of the frogs and the distant echo of that spirit’s violin note, already dreaming of the next ritual, the next circle, the next threshold waiting to be crossed.

On the last night of Celestine's life, the air was thick with thunder, but not a drop of rain fell. The sky was so black even the crows stayed in their nests. Zariah was fourteen, grown almost as tall as her mother, her limbs long and tensile as willow branches. She was supposed to be in bed, but she was too restless, pacing the dark corridor behind the front porch, ferrying crates of dried herbs and bottled river water, stacking them against the flaking white rail as her mother instructed.

Outside, beyond the dim glow of the porch lantern, voices rumbled. At first it was a familiar drone—the neighbors gossiping, as they sometimes did, about the Loa women and their uncanny ways. But tonight the sound had a fever in it, the kind that spread even among those who knew better. Shadows gathered at the edge of their property, torches popping and hissing in the heavy air, voices raised in anger and fear. A man Zariah recognized from the mill threw a stone that ricocheted off the porch post, landing with a clatter.

Celestine stood at the top of the steps, arms folded. Her robe was cinched tight, her face set and sharp as a hatchet. "Zari," she said, not turning, "fetch the salt and the white chalk. Bring that little jar with the red wax, too."

Zariah ducked into the parlor, hands shaking. She grabbed the sack of coarse salt, the short nubs of chalk, and the jar—she'd never seen this one opened before, and the wax smelled like scorched roses. When she returned, her mother was already on her knees, drawing a wide circle on the warped porch boards, her movements swift and deliberate. As the chalk touched the wood, Zariah felt a cool draft sweep across her bare feet, as if the porch boards themselves were exhaling.

The crowd drew closer, a snarling wall of firelight and hate. Another man, his face a mask of frenzied terror, tossed a glass bottle, and it shattered at the foot of the steps, spilling kerosene on the dirt. The reek of it stung Zariah's nose; she held the salt out, careful not to step on the freshly-drawn line.

Celestine took it, poured a thick border over the chalk, and began to chant, not loud but clear, the same cadence Zariah remembered from a hundred childhood nights. But tonight it was a weapon, not a comfort. The salt glowed with a faint, lambent energy, humming against the rising roar of the mob.
On the other side of the rail, faces burned in the light of their own torches—

neighbors, distant cousins, even the old preacher's wife, her mouth stretched in a high, screaming curse. At their head was Mama Laveau, the rival priestess Zariah had heard stories about since she was little. Laveau's eyes gleamed, her ashen hair wild in the wind, her mouth twisted into a snarl that showed all her teeth.

"We warned you, Celestine," Laveau said, her voice deep and serrated. "Told you and told you—stop mixing with the dead, stop bringing the shadows into the world." She pointed a crooked finger at Zariah, who shrank against the wall. "She's the worst of it. Born wrong, that one. Never should have been allowed to grow."

The porch was now a tiny island in a sea of firelight and hate. Zariah's hands were white-knuckled on the banister, her tongue too swollen to form words. Celestine just kept chanting, her words falling in steady rhythm, until even Laveau's voice was drowned by the drone.

A man surged up the steps, brandishing a hooked knife. The blade was stained black, and he moved with the loose, flailing grace of someone not entirely in control of his own limbs. Celestine did not flinch. She raised her arm, palm forward, and the circle's border glowed with a hot, electric purple.

But as she did, a dark, pulsing energy erupted from Mama Laveau’s hand, a serpentine whip of shadow and rage that struck the circle's glow. The porch boards groaned beneath them, and Celestine's chant faltered for just a moment. It was all the man needed. He lunged, his knife quick and desperate. Celestine twisted, but not enough, and the blade sank deep into her shoulder. A strange, burning chill radiated from the wound, far beyond the simple cut.

She gasped, then backhanded the man with such force he flew backward over the rail, crashing into the mob and knocking several people down with him. The air crackled with a flash of magical energy as he hit the ground.

Zariah was at her mother's side in an instant, her hand reaching out to catch her as she staggered. Blood soaked the shoulder of Celestine's robe, dark and spreading, but it was the unnatural pallor creeping across her mother's face that truly terrified Zariah. The poison was already taking hold. Celestine’s eyes went glassy, the pupils wide as moons, a sheen of sweat breaking out on her brow.
"Finish the line," Celestine hissed, her voice strained, pressing her own hand over the gash. "Don't let them break the circle."

Zariah grabbed the chalk, her knuckles scraping splinters, and dropped to her knees. Her hand was wild, but the chalk trembled with a life of its own, scrawling the final few feet of the sigil. As she completed the circle, something shifted. The porch boards vibrated beneath her knees, and the hair on her arms rose as if the air itself was electrified. The chant tumbled from her mouth, words she didn't even know she knew, ancient and powerful, and the air around the circle crackled with visible energy.

From the garden, a wind sprang up, sharp and sudden, tearing leaves from the trees and scattering rose petals and dust across the circle's surface. Laveau shrieked, voice cracking, her dark energy dissipating against the circle's renewed glow. "She's calling them! She's calling the dead!"

The air above the circle shimmered, and from the swirling mist, spectral hands reached out, skeletal fingers grasping at the air. Corpses, long buried, clawed their way from the earth of the garden, their eyes glowing with an eerie, otherworldly light. A low, guttural moan rose from their ranks, a sound that chilled Zariah to the bone.

One of the spectral figures, its face a rotting mask of what was once a kindly neighbor, floated towards the edge of the circle. It reached out a translucent hand, and the torch held by a man near the rail sputtered and went out, plunging him into darkness. He screamed, a choked, terrified sound, before collapsing. Zariah didn't see what happened, but she heard the wet tearing.

Another of the risen dead, its earthly wounds still visible, lunged at the man who had thrown the kerosene. Its spectral form passed through the wooden rail as if it weren't there, and the man clawed at his throat, his eyes bulging in horror, before he, too, fell silent.
Panic erupted in the mob. Several screamed and turned to flee, their torches scattered on the ground. But others, fueled by their rage and perhaps a belief in their numbers, hesitated.

Mama Laveau, her face a twisted mask of fury and fear, tried to unleash another blast of dark magic, but the sheer volume of spectral energy pouring from the circle overwhelmed her. Her spell fizzled and died in the air.

The risen dead turned their attention to the remaining townsfolk. Their movements were slow and jerky, but their touch was deadly. One woman, the old preacher's wife, who had screamed curses only moments before, was surrounded by three spectral figures. Their translucent hands reached for her, and her screams cut off abruptly.
Seeing the carnage, the remaining members of the mob finally broke and ran, their torches disappearing into the darkness. Mama Laveau, was among them, her face a mask of utter defeat and terror.

The porch was silent except for the two of them. The spectral forms spiraled around Zariah and Celestine, their silent moans filling the air. The torches on the lawn flickered and died, one by one, until only the faint, ethereal glow of the risen dead illuminated the scene. A thunderclap shook the sky. The wind died all at once, leaving behind only the chilling presence of the dead. Zariah dropped to her knees beside Celestine, who was now breathing in shallow, ragged gasps, her skin growing colder by the second. The poison was spreading quickly
Celestine's eyes found her daughter's, and she smiled, bloody teeth flashing. "You did good, Zari," she said, voice barely above a whisper. "You kept the line."
"Don't go," Zariah pleaded, pressing her hands to the wound, trying to stop the impossible.

Celestine's hand covered Zariah's, gentle and final. "All things got to go sometime. Even the river goes to meet the sea." she shivered slightly, “But I will love you even from the other side…” Her eyes closed, and with a long, rattling sigh, she let go.

For a while, Zariah just sat there, rocking her mother's body, blood soaking through her dress, the porch covered in a mess of salt, chalk, and rose petals. The moon never rose. In the distance, the bayou resumed its endless, indifferent croak of frogs.

The sun came up like a soft confession, bleeding slow and gold through the veils of Spanish moss. Zariah stood at the edge of her mother's grave, the hem of her black dress heavy with last night's dew.

Mourners clustered in small, uncertain knots beneath the oaks, linen and lace wilting in the sticky, predawn heat. They didn't meet her eyes for long; their gazes flicked away, restless, as if afraid the sight of her might draw more than just bad memories. They had seen what she had done, and they were afraid.

The pine coffin rested on two battered saw horses. The lid was closed, but Zariah could see the faintest curl of her mother's hair still snagged in the seam, like the tail of a comma at the end of a spell. The preacher, imported from a town downriver and paid in hush money and moonshine, prayed in a slow, looping Haitian Creole.

There were no hymns, no songs—just the steady pulse of the swamp, the click and shush of insects. A dozen candles burned along the grave's rim, their glass cups already filmed with sweat, wax pooling thick and white around the wicks. But their flames did not burn straight; they leaned inward, dancing and flickering as if a great, unseen force was drawing their light into the coffin itself.

When the prayers faded, the preacher nodded to Zariah. Her knees trembled, not with fear but with exhaustion, but she stepped forward and knelt beside the coffin. Her fingers traced the rough grain of the wood, then lingered on the carving—a crude river sigil Celestine made herself, years before, when she thought every good spell needed a signature.

For a long time, Zariah just knelt, head bowed. The world narrowed to the warmth of her mother's name in her mouth, the ache in her chest, the pulse in her wrists. She felt utterly alone, a child standing on the precipice of a world she had only just begun to understand.
She felt him before she saw him.

He stood just outside the circle of mourners, a silhouette half-made by the morning sun, leaning on a carved cane that looked as if it grew straight from the earth. His face was a lattice of lines, his beard white and curling, his coat as dark as midnight. He watched her, his gaze not unkind, but heavy with a patient, ancient grief. It was the look of a man who had seen many children kneel by many graves, and who had waited through all of them. His gaze lingered on the coffin for a moment, a profound, silent farewell that held a thousand years of love and loss.
Zariah felt his gaze, and when she looked up, he tipped his hat. The motion was almost imperceptible, yet as he did, a single candle at the coffin's head flared twice as bright, then went out.

He approached on silent feet, the thump of his cane lost in the crush of damp grass. He stopped at her shoulder and bent with an agility that belied his age. His breath smelled of black licorice and tobacco, his eyes so dark they reflected nothing but the glint of the candles.
He pressed something small and folded into Zariah's palm. She tensed, but the grip was gentle, almost grandfatherly.

"Crossroads always waiting, little queen," he said, his voice so low she wasn't sure anyone else heard it. "Every turn, every loss, every new name you take. Door's never shut for the likes of you. Not when you've got the road in your blood."
She stared at him, uncertain if she should thank him or curse him. But the old man only smiled, teeth strong and white, and straightened.
"They'll tell you to forget her," he murmured, his gaze sweeping the mourners, "but you know that's not how the world works."
He turned and walked away, cane tapping slow as a metronome. No one seemed to notice him go.
Zariah looked at her hand, opened it. The note was folded tight, and for a moment she considered not reading it at all. But curiosity was the one hunger she'd never been able to deny.
She opened the slip of paper. The writing was cramped, slanting, each letter tangled with flourishes that looked more like sigils than script.
‘You are not a mistake. She gave you the river, but I gave you the road. The name they try to steal, keep it close. The dead have more to say. Walk on.’
She felt the sudden, warm pressure of a hand on her shoulder—her mother's hand, strong and sure, a final, tangible touch.

She straightened, her back unbending. When the time came to lower the coffin, she stood back, her eyes dry and a new, quiet strength in her stance. The mourners watched her, wary and expectant. As the box sank, a wind picked up, sudden and strange, and the remaining candles all flickered, their flames briefly turning a vibrant, impossible blue.
When the preacher asked if anyone would like to say a word, Zariah did not hesitate.

"My mother was a rootworker and a healer," Zariah said, her voice steady and hard as bone, but with an undercurrent of new power. "She taught me that magic isn't for scaring people, or for making yourself more than them. It's for keeping a place in the world. For holding on, even when they try to scrub you out."
She looked up at the crowd, her gaze challenging, unafraid. "I aim to hold on."

There was a long, ragged silence. Then, quietly, the crowd dispersed, one or two at a time, their fear of her now a quiet, terrified understanding. Zariah stood over the grave until she was alone, the leaves overhead dripping slow tears onto the fresh, upturned soil.

As she turned to leave, a crow cawed once, sharp and insistent. It was a final, knowing farewell, a promise whispered on the wind. She glanced over her shoulder, half expecting to see the old man waiting at the edge of the woods, but there was nothing—just the empty graveyard, and the promise of a crossroads somewhere up ahead.

p: The morning Zariah left the bayou, the sky was bruised plum and orange sherbet, the kind of dawn that promised storms by nightfall. She arrived in New Orleans with her life in a canvas satchel—vials of salt, her mother's pocketknife, dried rose petals, and the folded note from the crossroads man. She felt less like a traveler and more like a ghost, a hollow ache in her chest where her home used to be. The city was a different world. Neon sputtered from every bar and bodega; the air carried the double perfume of spilled bourbon and rotting jasmine.

She rented a back room in the French Quarter from a woman named Madame Toussaint, who never left her chair by the window. The room was barely bigger than a closet, but it was all Zariah could afford. For the first few nights, she lay on the cot stuffed with Spanish moss, clutching the note in her hand, the words a silent promise that felt more like a curse. She hummed her mother's tune, but her voice was a thin, reedy thing, hollow and lost.
On her fourth night, a storm finally broke. Rain fell in sheets, and the wind howled like a banshee. Just after midnight, a frantic banging on her door startled her from a fitful sleep.
When she opened it, a pack of street kids stood huddled in the rain, their faces streaked with dirt and fear. They were holding something limp and whimpering, its fur matted with rain and blood.
"Please, Mambo Z," one of them pleaded, using the name the city was already whispering. "He needs you."

Zariah looked at the dog, a half-starved mutt, its jaw split in two and hanging at a gruesome angle. The kids had come to her, not to a vet. They had heard the whispers, but she felt like a fraud. She was just a girl with a satchel of herbs and a broken heart. Her hands, which had so recently put her mother to rest, felt small and useless.

But as she hesitated, her gaze fell on the old, scarred pocketknife tucked into her satchel. The initials "C.L." were carved into the bone handle. A voice, clear as a bell but not her own, echoed in her mind: "Magic isn't for scaring people, or for making yourself more than them. It's for keeping a place in the world."
She stepped aside and let them in.

The children watched in a hushed circle as Zariah went to work. She cleaned the wound with bottled river water and began to hum her mother's song, her voice now steady and sure. She mixed river clay with powerful herbs, a poultice that pulsed with a faint, green light, and smeared it across the broken bone. She had never done anything this complex, not without her mother's guidance. The wound was too severe for simple poultices and whispered words. She needed something more.

With a sudden, fierce resolve, she pulled the pocketknife from her satchel and nicked her own thumb. A single drop of blood fell onto the clay, and the poultice flared, a blinding flash of green and gold light. The dog whimpered, its brown eyes rolling with pain, but Zariah’s hands held it fast, whispering to the beast as its shattered jaw slowly, agonizingly, began to fuse.

The rain beat against the windows, the thunder shook the house, but in the small room, there was only the low hum of Zariah's magic and the rhythmic, steady pulse of the clay. All night she worked, her hands a blur of motion, her focus absolute.

At dawn, the storm subsided. The dog, its jaw now fused as if it had never broken, was sleeping soundly on her cot, its tongue lolling. The children, exhausted but overjoyed, paid her with two cigarettes and a chunk of honeycomb wrapped in newspaper. They called her a miracle worker, but she just smiled, a sharp, humorless curve of her lips that was all business and no joy.

She sent them on their way, saying not to come bother her again, and stood in the doorway, watching the city awaken. The air smelled of wet asphalt and fresh bread, and the morning light was a soft, pale gold. She looked down at her hands. They were no longer trembling. They were stained with mud and blood, but they felt strong. She had carried the weight of her mother's legacy, and she had not broken.
In that small, quiet moment, the girl who had fled the bayou died. And from her ashes, Mambo Z, the witch who walked the edges, was born.

Night in the Quarter was a beast that wouldn't be tamed—too many people, too many secrets, all of it crackling beneath the thin crust of the neon. Zariah stood on her balcony, three stories above Bourbon, arms braced on the curling ironwork. She breathed in the cocktail of beer and jasmine and fried dough and felt the pulse of the city as if it were her own restless blood. The moon was a thin coin, sharp-edged and false as a promise. Down in the street, the party was eternal, but up here the air tasted cooler, cleaner.

She'd never been good at stillness. Usually, when the city slept, she stalked it; but tonight something kept her pinned. The hum of the crowd drifted upward in little bursts—shouts, laughter, a brass band winding down a block away.

She was just about to go inside—there was a book and half a bottle of rye waiting for her—when she sensed the shift. A subtle thickening in the shadows behind her, a hush that felt like someone holding their breath. Zariah didn't turn. She'd learned the rules of this world: sometimes it was better to let the story walk up on its own.
"Do you know the riddle about the morning, the noon, and the dusk?" said a voice, low and warm as spiced rum. The words rolled out like a conjure, wrapping her in their rhythm.
She grinned. "That's the oldest one in the book, sugar. Man walks on four legs as a baby, two as a man, three with a cane when he's old."

There was a small, pleased sound behind her, and then the stranger stepped into the moonlight. He was tall, whip-thin, his coat black and old-fashioned, cut long and close. His eyes were amber, sharp and bright as a predator's.
"Some say the classics are worth repeating," he said, bowing slightly. "But you already know all the classics. So why bother with the obvious?"
She snorted, not unkindly. "Maybe because nobody likes a show-off."

He leaned against the rail beside her, hands folded neatly. His skin was dark and gleaming, his hair cropped tight and neat. There was something uncanny about the way he stood—like a marionette whose strings were being pulled just a little too carefully. Up close, the scent of him was not quite right: not sweat or cologne, but the dry, electric smell of summer pavement after the first drop of rain.
"Maybe I'm here to be shown up," he said, voice gone sly. "Or maybe I'm here to see if you're as sharp as they say, Mambo Z."
She arched a brow. "And who's they, exactly? You got a fan club I don't know about?"
His smile widened, exposing a flash of gold in his teeth. "Every legend has its observers."

They stood in silence for a moment, watching the blur of tourists below. Zariah tried to pinpoint what it was about him that kept drawing her eye. Maybe it was the way he never blinked. Maybe it was the stillness, the sense that he was coiled and waiting for something even as he seemed perfectly at ease.
"You got a name, stranger?" she asked at last.
He gave her a look, as if weighing her, then said, "You can call me Anansi."
Zariah whistled, low. "Like the spider?"
"Just so." He ran a finger along the railing, drawing invisible lines. "I like stories, and the people who spin them. Seems to me you're both, these days."
She laughed, sharp and short. "I just fix what's broken, that's all. If people want to call it magic, let 'em."
Anansi cocked his head, considering. "You believe in the old ways. Even when nobody else does."
She shrugged. "If it works, it works. End of story."

A lull in the noise below; a small group of men staggered out of a bar, arms around each other's shoulders, singing off-key and happy. Zariah watched them go, their joy infectious even from three stories up.
Anansi followed her gaze. "Ever think about what's left when the party's over?" he asked. "Who sweeps the floors, who wipes the tables, who remembers the songs?"
She snorted. "I figure the stories remember themselves. If not, someone else will come along and invent a better one."
He laughed, "Now, that is a philosophy I can respect."

They talked through the night, voices drifting over the rail and down into the soft, blue dark. They traded riddles and old stories, half-truths and lies; Zariah held her own, deflecting the questions that cut too close, but sometimes she let something slip—a memory of her mother, a trick from the old days, a wish she thought she'd buried.
At some point, Anansi produced a flask from his coat and offered her a sip. It burned and soothed in equal measure. She drank, then handed it back. "You always carry that?" she asked.
"Only when I expect company," he said, and there was a sincerity in his eyes.

Dawn came slow, like the end of a long, good song. The city softened, the shrieks and horns and music fading into something quiet and sweet. Zariah glanced sideways, expecting him to be gone—another trick of the night—but Anansi was still there, staring at the pale horizon, his grin softer now, almost wistful.
"I'll be seeing you," he said, and in the next blink, he'd vanished, leaving only the ghost of his laughter in the air.

Zariah stood on the balcony for a long time, her arms crossed over her chest, the taste of rum and riddles still on her tongue. She watched the sunlight climb the side of St. Louis Cathedral and felt, for the first time in years, that she wasn't alone in the world. She'd never been good at stillness, but now she thought she could try to learn.

ch.src: Sebastian Nightwell and Thaddeus Johnson, Heart of the Drakkyn (2025), Chapter 22
p: The first rule of a midnight council: do not show weakness, not even to the dead.

In the parlor of Zariah Loa's new home—a disreputable mansion on the wrong end of Royal, bones of the old city's colonial rot poking through in every ceiling rose and cracked marble tile—the air was syrupy with beeswax and blue tobacco smoke. She had painted the walls herself, tracing great vevé sigils in layers of limewash and ash, so every guest who entered felt the tickle of old magic along their skin, the sense of being weighed by a hundred watching ancestors.

That night, every chair and divan was packed. The gathering was more than Zariah had expected, but she would not admit to nerves, not with so many eyes on her. The candlelight amplified every movement, every stray glance. Vampires in tailored silks and bone-white linen sprawled like pashas along the velvet settees, eyes agleam with anticipation. Across from them, three ghosts clustered in a sulk of gauzy shrouds, lips pursed, their silver chain fetters pooled on the floor like spilled mercury. The shifters—still mostly human in this form—leaned against the fireplace, radiating a wet-dog musk that made the vampires shift, restless, on their cushions.

Zariah stood before her throne. It was a battered, gold-leafed thing she had purchased from a Bourbon Street bazaar, its upholstery faded to the color of dried blood, the legs lacquered black and clawed as a panther's paw.

She wore her best: a dress cut from midnight velvet and trailing belladonna blooms, bare feet laced with river-mud and fine silver chains. Her hair was up, twisted tight and crowned with a cluster of crow feathers. Her eyes, dark as bayou mud after a storm, flicked across the room and dared anyone to challenge her right to sit.
A tap on the crystal goblet at her side brought hush. The crowd leaned in, predator and prey distinctions blurred for the night.

"Tonight," she began, voice pitched to fill the room but not strain it, "we gather as equals. Not as predator or haunt or child of the moon, but as folk of this city, bound by a need for peace and power."
A ghost snickered—an old Creole matron with pearls layered high enough to choke her twice over. "Peace is a lie," she said, not unkindly. "But power, that's a word worth chewing."
Zariah nodded. "Then let's chew it together."
A shapeshifter with mottled eyes—part wolf, part something else—slid forward, hands in pockets. "Is it true what they say? That the Mambo's house is neutral ground?"

"Tonight it is," Zariah said. "And every night hence, so long as you respect the circle." She gestured, and the candle flames guttered for a moment, then flared blue. The vevé on the walls pulsed, visible for just a heartbeat—a flicker that set every hair on the back of every neck to quivering.

A vampire, impossibly handsome in the way of movie stars or super models, raised a glass. "To the new queen, then. May her rules be better than her predecessors'." The toast was echoed, some with sarcasm, some with genuine hunger.

She claimed her seat at last, the velvet sucking in a sigh as she settled. The council resumed: grudges aired, old alliances reaffirmed, gossip traded with the sharp efficiency of wolves dissecting a carcass. For an hour, Zariah listened, interjected only to settle disputes with a single, measured word. Her reputation was still untested, but the legend grew with every moment she refused to flinch.

At midnight, a child appeared at the edge of the parlor—a little thing, maybe seven, with eyes the color of storm-water and skin blanched near gray. No one claimed her, though the crowd parted as she stumbled in. Her limbs jerked in sudden, ugly spasms; her head snapped side to side as if listening to voices no one else could hear.

Zariah was out of her seat before anyone could move. She knelt by the child, who had collapsed onto a rug woven with violets and brass thread. The girl was cold as a carp, breath shallow and quick as moth wings.
Zariah put a hand to the girl's cheek, then reached into her apron for the little glass vials she kept hidden there—river-water, honeyed clay, a sprig of mint dipped in the last moon's light.

She dabbed the child's lips with the mint, murmured a low, riverine spell. The shivering slowed. Zariah slipped a thumb into the space behind the child's ear and traced a spiral, an old Loa mark—one meant for banishing fever demons, or the spirits that sometimes tried to nest inside the living. A pulse of heat swept the child's body, enough that the nearest ghost recoiled.
"Ancestry?" Zariah asked, not looking up.
"D'Aubigny, I think," said a voice from the corner. "Mother's side, at least, body snatcher blood."

Zariah lifted the girl's hand, examined the tiny blue veins, the way the fingers curled as if gripping an invisible reed. She recited the d'Aubigny ward, layering it over her own healing rune, and felt the resistance—an oily, unwilling spirit clinging to the girl's spine.

The council watched, hungry and silent, as Zariah leaned close to the child's ear and whispered, "You don't belong here. Go back to the mud. Go back to the dark." She drew her pocketknife, sliced her own palm, and let a single drop of blood fall onto the girl's brow.
The effect was instant. The child arched, gasped, then sagged into Zariah's lap, breathing slow and even. The foreign spirit—dark, reptilian, ancient—
boiled out of her mouth in a streak of shadow and disappeared through the floorboards. A long, collective shiver ran through the room.
Zariah cradled the child until her color returned, then passed her to a waiting servant in a white coat, who hustled her out with the efficiency of someone used to such displays.
The council erupted—questions, accusations, a few curses tossed like confetti. But Zariah held up her bleeding hand, and the room stilled.
"She's under my protection now," she said. "Like all of you. If you want to test that, you know where to find me."
No one did. Not that night, not for a long time after.

As the council adjourned—ghosts melting through the walls, vampires vanishing into the rain, shifters slipping away one by one—Zariah remained on her throne, hands folded, watching the last of the blue candle burn itself to nothing.
In the hush that followed, she thought of her mother's hands—callused, scarred, always gentle—and wondered if they would recognize the woman she had become.

That night, the heat was a living thing. It pushed in through the open windows, slicked the walls with sweat and night-blooming jasmine. Even the ghosts in the parlor had gone elsewhere, seeking shade or trouble. Zariah stood in her courtyard, toes curled into the cracks of ancient tile, silk robe loose at her hips, hair down and wild.
The moon burned a white hole in the sky. It glanced off her dressing mirror

—an antique, brass-framed slab salvaged from a Bourbon Street brothel, now propped against the crumbling garden wall. She was watching her reflection, but also watching the dark beyond it, the thick tangle of vines and wrought iron gate that guarded her bit of green from the city's hungers.
Something moved on the far side of the gate. Not a shadow, not a cat, but a shape she knew by the way it leaned into the light, curious and hungry.
"Found you, little queen," said the voice, warm as rum on a winter morning.

Anansi stepped from the darkness, coat gleaming wet and black, shirt crisp, shoes the color of split walnut. Slung over one shoulder, he carried a satchel that writhed and shifted as if it were packed with something alive—or, more likely, a thousand someones, tangled up together and trying to escape.
He bowed, exaggerated, the top of his head nearly touching his knees. "You summon me?"
Zariah grinned, arms crossed under her breasts. "Didn't know I had to. I figured you'd show up once the moon got good and weird."
He stepped closer, slipping through the bars as if he were made of fog, the wrought iron wincing at his touch. The air between them sparked, a tension that was part warning, part invitation.
"You ever get tired of stories, Anansi?" she asked.
He tilted his head. "Only the ones with sad endings."
"Good thing I haven't written mine yet."

She let him come to her. He smelled like burnt sugar and the sweet black rot of river mud in August. His hands were cool on her waist, fingers long and knowing. He lifted her, just a little, and spun her so that she was facing the mirror. They stood together, twin reflections in the glass.

He leaned in close, his mouth a whisper against her ear. "Your father gave you the road, little queen, but your mother's story is tangled within it. I came to tell you... the truth is a lie waiting to happen."
She stared at his reflection, her heart hammering, not with fear but with the thrill of the chase.

They moved to the table under the magnolia tree, its branches heavy with fat white blooms. He poured her a drink—something sharp and honeyed—and they traded stories, true and false, beneath the thick canopy of scent and shadow. She told him about the graveyard, about the street kids and the dog; he listened, nodded, spun her tale into something grander, mythic, his words gilding the edges of her memory.
He leaned across the table. "You know why the old stories last so long?"
"Because nobody ever gets the answer right?" she teased.
He shook his head, slow and deliberate. "Because the ending keeps changing."

The moon climbed higher. The city's noise receded until there was nothing but the scrape of cicadas and their shared breath. He kissed her, gentle at first, then with a hunger that made her knees buckle. They found their way to her bed, limbs tangled, lips bruising, stories and lies and laughter falling away until there was only the honest language of bodies.

In the dark, he traced lines along her back, whispering secrets and promises. She pressed him down, her hand at his throat, and he laughed, the sound spilling over into something needy and sweet. He tasted of molasses and ancient dust, of all the places she had never been.

When it was over—or as close to over as these things got—she woke to find the sheets cold, Anansi gone. The only sign of him was a single, impossibly fine thread, now a line of silver running from the foot of her bed to the front door, and out through the wrought iron gate.
She stared at the thread, heart hammering, then lifted her hand and traced the path it took, slow and deliberate, as if she might someday follow it to its end.

The room was a cube—nothing more, nothing less. Cement on all sides, cold as a butcher's slab. The only break in the geometry: a wall of iron bars, each etched with runes that glowed, faint and nauseating, under the punishing wash of overhead fluorescents.

Zariah sat cross-legged in the center of the floor, as if by cultic design. She wore state-issue scrubs, dyed a color best described as "regret." Her hands rested lightly on her knees, palms up, fingers curled.
A camera hummed in the corner. Zariah looked up at it, then stuck out her tongue. The machine blinked once, recording.
Behind the mirror—one-way, because of course it was—Dr. Verrin and Dr. Vex watched her.
"She's not even trying to breach," said Verrin. He said it like a diagnosis, disappointment layered over pride.
"She's conserving," said Vex. "Like she's waiting for something. Or someone."

The doctor ran his finger along the clipboard, then stabbed at a button on the desk. On Zariah's side of the mirror, the lights blared twice as bright, then faded back to cruel. She squinted, but did not flinch. "Ya’ll got any more tricks, sugar?" she muttered, eyes closed now, voice low.

She hummed a note, not quite a song, but a sound that vibrated the fillings in her teeth. In the back of her skull, she felt the pulse of the wards—there, there, and there, each rune designed to sting the Loa like a thousand glass splinters. She ran her mind across them, the way her mother had taught her to test a fence: gentle, patient, looking for rust or fault.
One bar, the third from the left, stuttered its red glow when she breathed the right syllable. She filed this away. If you could make a thing, you could break it.
Verrin's voice, piped through the intercom: "Ms. Loa. We need you to participate in another diagnostic. You will feel a mild sedative, then an auditory cue. Please do not resist."
"Or what?" Zariah asked, opening her eyes.
There was a pause on the other side. Then: "It will hurt."
She shrugged, then leaned back, rolling her neck until the vertebrae popped. "Pain it’s just a riddle with no manners," she said, to no one.

A hiss. She felt the sedative in her spine, crawling up like frostbite. Her vision narrowed, whited out, then came back double, then triple. She was no longer on the floor. She was on a porch somewhere humid, the air dripping with honeysuckle and the memory of a woman's laugh. Her mother, young and beautiful, hair up in a scarf, mixing something in a chipped enamel bowl.
"Wake up, Zari," said the ghost of her mother. "Can't let them steal your stories."
Zariah gasped, and the world slammed back into the cell, into the cube, into the ache of her bones on cold cement.
She tasted blood. She grinned, lips split and wet. "That all you got?" she spat at the mirror.

Dr. Vex's face flickered into view behind the glass. She spoke, voice a candysickly sing-song: "Such bravado, Queen Zariah. You know, the last demigod we caught, while quite resilient, begged for death before the end of week one."
Zariah lifted a brow, "Oh? So your methods suck..."
Vex cackled, the sound like a hyena choking on bone. She slapped the clipboard, then stormed away. Verrin lingered, just a shape in the glass, hands folded, waiting for Zariah to make the next move.
Hours passed. They did not feed her. The lights cycled from hard to harder. Zariah counted the seconds in batches of four hundred, singing under her breath.

Midnight, or something close to it, the air shifted. A spider, big as a plum and shiny as obsidian, lowered itself from the corner of the ceiling on a thread of purest silver. Its back was marked with a tangle of white lines, the pattern familiar and dear—a web, and inside the web, a secret.
Zariah's heart jumped, but her face was cool. She slid forward on her knees, level with the spider.
"Been a minute, Anansi," she whispered.
The spider scuttled closer, the air around it warping, just a little. Zariah leaned in, and the world blurred at the edges.
Anansi's voice was not a sound, exactly, but it ran through her head with the comfort of a song learned by heart. "You ready to go home, little queen?"
Zariah laughed, just a whisper. "Got a plan?"
The spider's legs vibrated. "I always have a plan. But you have to want it more than they do."
She thought of the runes, the stuttering glow, the rust in the magic that held her here. She thought of her mother, the river, the promise she had made at the edge of a grave.
"I want it," she said, and in the low light, the spider glowed brighter.
On the other side of the mirror, Verrin leaned in, curiosity tickling the edge of his composure. "What is she doing?" he whispered. No one answered.
The spider vibrated again. "Then let's get to work, my heart. This story's only half told."

ch.src: Sebastian Nightwell and Thaddeus Johnson, Heart of the Drakkyn (2025), Chapter 23
p: The wind gnawed, relentless, as the party climbed the switchbacked trails of the White Mountain foothills. Each step drove a knife of cold through Drake's sodden boots, up his calves, burrowing toward the brittle shell of his core. He tried to keep a rhythm—left, right, breathe, but the air was too thin to permit the old, easy flow. Even at midday, frost haloed every exhale.

Lyra was the first to fall behind. She tried to hide her misery, flitting at intervals between the tail of the pack and the low scrub pines that dotted the slope, but it was plain: the delicate wings folded to her spine trembled with every shudder of the wind. Her breathing came in desperate, ragged gasps.

Drake called a halt at a shallow alcove in the mountainside. He had learned not to wait for Cassian to advise; Cassian's advice arrived in the soundless looks he cast up and down the line, the way his hand found Drake's elbow to steady him, never possessive, always present.
"Ten minutes, everyone. Drink. Eat something," Drake said, voice rasping against the cold.

Elliana was at his shoulder in an instant, already shedding her pack and sliding down a lichen-stained boulder to scout their exposed flank. "This ridge will keep us in sight for another half hour, maybe less," she said. "After that, the scree run gets real hairy. I'll check for the best path."
Drake nodded, then squatted beside Lyra, who had collapsed, shivering, to her knees.
"You're not gonna die," he said. "At least not here."
She bared her teeth, half grin, half baring of fangs. "Isn't that always what people think, right before somethin' comes down from the sky and pecks yer head clean off?"

"You're thinking of crows. The crows don't live this high up," Cassian said, materializing behind Drake and offering a cracked tin of dried apricots to Lyra. He kept his own gloves on as he did, in this cold, even a moment of exposed flesh could be catastrophic.

Lyra popped an apricot in her mouth and chewed sullenly. "I heard about mountain crows once. Big as terriers, they were. Red eyes, claws like knives. Eat the eyeballs right out of yer skull, quick as ye please."

Drake couldn't help it—he laughed, a sound so loud and alien in the hush that even Elliana glanced back, lips quirking. "If anything comes for our eyeballs, you have my permission to use me as a human shield," he said. "I doubt they'll get much flavor out of me, anyway."

Lyra's laugh was weak, but real. She leaned her head on Drake's shoulder for a moment before Cassian gently guided her to sit upright, handing her a dented flask of spiced tea. The warmth hit her lips, and her eyes fluttered closed in relief.

There was no rest for Elliana. She was already picking her way along the next section, eyes squinted against the brightness, boot edges grinding on frozen gravel. Drake watched her, trying to see what she saw. To his left, the slope fell away into a chasm, the kind of depth that made his stomach turn. Above, sheer faces of rock swept upward into the sun, blinding white and blue, so bright it erased all detail. In the sharp-edged shadows, the world was black and flat as paper.

He hated this—he hated the cold, the uncertainty, the ever-present threat of falling, but most of all he hated how easily the mountain stripped away every illusion of strength. Here, nobody was anything but muscle, bone, and whatever grit they could scrounge up against the wind.
Cassian caught him watching Elliana. "She's not going to fall," he said, voice pitched low so only Drake could hear. "She's got the lightest feet of anyone I've ever met."

Drake wanted to say something clever—he always did—but his lips were numb, and the wind carried away the words before he could shape them. Instead, he nodded, then turned his gaze to Cassian's hands, where they were peeling an orange, the skin coiling in perfect spirals onto a handkerchief.
"Where'd you learn to do that?" Drake asked, nodding at the orange.

Cassian smiled—small, almost secret. "My father used to say you could tell a man's character by the way he peeled fruit. Neatness, patience, respect for the shape of things." He offered Drake a wedge, which Drake took, savoring the sweet juice.

Elliana returned, her cheeks flushed and her eyes bright, more alive than anyone had a right to be at this altitude. "I found a cut-through. We'll have to skirt a bit of loose snow, but it's faster than taking the goat path. Less risk of avalanche."
Lyra groaned. "Yeah… and that's what they always say right before it comes crashin' down."
"Have faith," Elliana said, grinning, and tugged Drake up by his armpit.
“Aye, an there’s another!”

They shouldered packs and moved out, Elliana leading at a measured pace that minimized the risk of slips but kept them just at the edge of what Lyra could handle. Drake brought up the rear now, determined not to let anyone lag behind. He watched Lyra's back, the way her wings twitched with every sudden gust, the tiny ice crystals that gathered at the tips and clinked together as she moved.

They moved in silence, mostly. In these conditions, conversation was both a luxury and a liability; every breath was precious. Only when they rounded a bluff and caught their first glimpse of the Western Heart, the entrance to the dwarven stronghold—still miles away, but glowing faintly in the low sun—did the hush break.
"Holy shite," Lyra muttered, then louder: "I can feel it from here. Like a nice home hearth, warm as ye please."

At first, he thought it was just the afterimage of the sun: a vein of gemstone, running straight through the cliff face, pulsing with blue and gold fire. The fortress itself was half-hidden by the curve of the rock, but even at this distance, Drake felt the warmth of the furnaces within.
Cassian laid a hand on Drake's shoulder, steadying him. "They say the dwarves mine with their ears," he said. "They listen for the soul in the stone."
"I hope they're friendly," Lyra said. "Because I cannae run at this altitude, not one bit."

Elliana gestured for them to stop. She crouched, then motioned for Drake and Cassian to join her. "The entrance is at the base of that outcrop," she said, pointing to a shelf of ice and crystal that jutted from the mountain like a broken tooth. "We'll have to descend about thirty meters, then double back along the ledge. If you're not careful—" she drew a line in the air, tracing the fall—"it's a straight drop to the river."
Lyra whistled. "So, no pressure then, aye."

They made the descent roped together, Cassian at the anchor, Elliana leading. The rope bit into Drake's hips, but he was grateful for the security; the wind was worse here, and every step felt like it might be his last. Lyra nearly slipped twice, but each time Elliana was there, hand outstretched, never judgmental, just matter-of-fact.

The ledge narrowed. Below, Drake saw the river, frozen in places, black and winding through the ravine. The wind slapped at him, and for a moment he was certain he would go over. Cassian was the only thing that kept him rooted, the consistent guidance and support, the calm voice above: "Three more steps. Then left. Good."

When they reached the shelf, Lyra collapsed onto the snow and laughed, a sound equal parts hysteria and relief. Drake flopped beside her, panting, and only then did he notice the tremor in Cassian's hands as he coiled the rope.

Elliana, for her part, was already scanning the horizon, eyes locked on the giant stone gateway that marked the entrance to the Western Heart. She gestured them forward, and they trudged the last hundred yards in single file, boots crunching on the hard-packed snow.

They scrambled to the structure, teeth chattering, fingers barely functional. The entrance was guarded—not by men, but by what looked like a wall of metal, shot through with gleaming veins of crystal. At its center, a gate: forged from hammered iron and embossed with dwarven glyphs that pulsed, alive, as they approached.
Two dwarves—each barely five feet but wide as oxen, armored head to toe—
stepped from alcoves flanking the gate. Their helmets were crowned with spikes of gemstone; their faces were lost behind veils of steel mesh.
"State your business," one rumbled, voice so deep it vibrated Drake's bones.
Elliana stepped forward, hands raised. "We seek audience with the high smith of the Western Heart. We are on a mission of great importance.
The dwarves exchanged a look, then one signaled with a gauntlet, and the gate ground open, just enough for them to pass single-file.

Inside, the air was instantly warmer. The walls glowed with embedded crystals, casting a surreal light that softened the edges of everything. Drake stumbled, still dizzy, but Cassian was there, arm around his waist.
"Welcome to the Heart," Cassian said, voice hushed.
Drake wanted to say something—thanks, maybe, or just a word to fill the empty, echoing space—but instead he let himself lean against Cassian, just for a second, as the doors rumbled shut behind them.
In the dark, for the first time since the climb had begun, Drake allowed himself to believe they might actually survive this.

A corridor of raw stone and hammered steel stretched ahead, wider than any avenue in Dallas, and far more dangerous. Every surface glowed with a thousand points of artificial light—candles, burning minerals, tiny crystal filaments woven into the seams between stones. The effect was dazzling, a constellated sky folded down into the earth's black belly.

The dwarven guards ushered the party forward at a pace just short of a march, the clatter of boots echoing in the emptiness. Every dozen steps, another pair of sentries emerged from shadowed alcoves, each set more ornately armored than the last. Their eyes never left the party; not hostile, but deeply, implacably alert.

Drake's first impression was of heat, so different from the biting cold outside that his face prickled with sweat even as his hands remained numb. The smell was stone and metal and fire. They passed a side passage and Drake glimpsed the source: a forge the size of a public swimming pool, dwarves working in synchronized silence, hammers rising and falling with perfect rhythm. The walls of the forge glowed red, veins of molten ore tracing through the masonry like arteries pumping blood.
Lyra inhaled, her breath shivering with delight. "Oh, I could live here. If I didnae suffocate first, that is."
"Don't touch anything," Elliana murmured, too low for the dwarves to hear. "And if you must speak, stick to the script."
Drake wiped his forehead with a sleeve. "What script?"
Elliana's eyes flicked up, calculating. "Say as little as possible. If you must, compliment the stonework or the symmetry. That's how they measure worth."

They were herded deeper, down a spiraling ramp that seemed designed to intimidate. The walls here were inlaid with crystal plaques—some rectangular, some jagged as lightning—each inscribed with names and diagrams in a language Drake couldn't parse. Cassian lingered at the edge of the procession, occasionally slowing to trace a finger along a particularly dense knot of runes.
"What does it say?" Drake whispered, unable to help himself.
Cassian's brow creased. "It's a map. Or a ledger. I can't read the script, but the patterns repeat every third panel. It's… beautiful."
Drake wanted to ask what that meant, but Elliana gave him a look, and he shut up.

After a dizzying descent, they emerged into a hall so vast it humbled the memory of any cathedral Drake had ever seen. The ceiling arched so high it vanished into darkness, pierced only by the cool blue glow of massive stalactite chandeliers. The floor was polished obsidian, so perfectly reflective that every step appeared doubled, as if the world set at a second, inverted reality.

At the far end stood a dais of solid granite. A single figure awaited there: a dwarf of immense girth and height, his beard a river of silver, every plait secured with a different rune-etched clasp. He wore a cape of dark fur, its collar rising to frame his face in a mane, and his bare arms were as thick as Drake's thighs, corded with muscle and tattooed with curling script.
Lyra leaned in, voice trembling with awe: "That's Vorgat Hammerfist. He's the Ironspine Chief."
Elliana gave a nearly invisible nod. "Bow. Low. On my count."

They stopped at the appointed line, a band of inlaid gold across the floor. The dwarven guards peeled off, lining the perimeter in symmetrical rows. Elliana set the pace: right foot forward, left knee down, right fist to breastbone, head bowed. Drake copied, as did Cassian; Lyra made a valiant effort but wobbled, then exaggerated her posture in the hope of covering the mistake.
The silence was total, so oppressive that Drake's ears rang. Then, from the dais, the Ironspine Chief spoke:
"Visitors," he intoned, and his voice rumbled through the chamber like a quarry blast. "You claim a mission of import. Speak your intent."
Elliana rose from her bow, but kept her head lowered. "We seek the Soul Anchor, noble Chief. We are bound by the contract of the old realms—by right and by need."
A murmur passed among the guards. Drake saw a couple of them flex their fists, as if readying for a fight.
Vorgat's eyes narrowed, weighing them. "No one touches the Soul Anchor without the council's will. No one. This is known."
Elliana opened her hands, palms up, a gesture of peace. "We ask only for audience. Let the council hear our plea."
Vorgat grunted, unimpressed. "You come from the dragon's brood?" His gaze landed on Drake, studying the unnatural gleam of his eyes.
Drake straightened. "I am Drake Veridian, of Dallas Texas, half drakkyn and the prophecy’s child of scales.
The room was quiet enough to hear the intake of every dwarf in the chamber.
Cassian stepped forward, clearing his throat. "And I am Cassian Everhart, human of the High Scholarium of the Arcane Tower, bonded to this party by the pledge of the Three Moons."
The great room went quiet as the introductions were considered.
Lyra, never able to let a silence linger, piped up: "I'm Lyra Moondancer, and I'm… just here to help." Her voice went squeaky at the end. "I like yer chandeliers."
There was a ripple of laughter among the youngest guards, quickly stifled.
Elliana introduced herself last, with a flourish and a dip of the head. "Elliana Lampros, on contract to House Goldmantle, by the blood oath of the Forgelands."
Vorgat's brows rose, impressed despite himself. "We will see," he said.

He gestured, and attendants shuffled forward with a tray of hammered metal cups. The liquid within was a color Drake had never seen before—iridescent, shifting between blue and gold with the tilt of the hand. Each cup was presented to one of the party; Drake received his from a dwarf whose face was obscured by a cascade of hair and a helmet that looked a bit large.
"Drink," Vorgat commanded. "In this hall, no business can be spoken with a dry tongue."
Drake glanced at Cassian, who nodded, then at Lyra, who was already sniffing hers.
"To your health," Drake said, and downed the shot.

The burn was immediate and seismic. It ran up his nose and exploded behind his eyes, then flooded his chest with a fire that was oddly… comforting. He blinked, and for a moment, the runes on the walls seemed to hover and drift, patterns rearranging themselves into new forms.
Cassian drank more slowly, eyes fluttering closed as he swallowed. "I think I can read the runes now," he whispered, then shook his head as if clearing a dream.
Lyra's eyes watered; she coughed once, then wiped her mouth on her sleeve. "Tastes like someone dissolved a lightnin' bug in vodka," she stage-whispered to Elliana, who snorted.

Vorgat waited until they finished, then leaned forward on the dais. "You ask for the Soul Anchor. That is not a thing done lightly. The artifact does not belong to me alone; it belongs to the council of Seven Clans. To claim it, you must earn the right to be heard."
Drake felt the weight of every eye on him, but he did not look away.
"Then let us speak," he said, voice stronger than he felt. "We know the risks. But we also know the cost of waiting. The world above is changing. If we don't act, neither realm will survive."
There was a long pause. The words seemed to hang in the air, refracted by the heat and the glow of the crystals. Then Vorgat lifted his cup and drained it, slamming it down with a thunderclap.
"Tomorrow, you will address the full council," he declared. "But tonight, you rest. You are not prisoners, but guests. Guards will show you to your quarters."
The formal dismissal was clear, and Elliana bowed again, her fist to her heart. The others followed suit, then were escorted out by a different set of guards—
these in lighter armor, faces visible, curiosity barely hidden.
Once out of earshot, Lyra let out a low, whistling breath. "That was less horrible than I expected," she said.
"They're testing us," Elliana murmured. "Every word, every gesture."
"Are we passing?" Drake asked.
Elliana's eyes were opaque in the light, unreadable. "So far."

Their guest quarters were carved from a single boulder of granite, but lined with fur and hung with tapestries depicting ancient battles, mining expeditions, and what Drake suspected were drunken feasts. There was food waiting: dense bread, cured meats, pickled mushrooms, and more of the strange liquor.
Drake sat on the edge of his bunk, unsure what to do with himself now that the adrenaline was wearing off. Cassian hovered at the door, scanning for traps or enchantments.
"You okay?" Cassian asked, voice soft.
Drake shrugged, staring at his hands. "I'm not sure I'll ever be okay again."
Cassian sat beside him. "You did well in there. They respect strength. Even if it's just the strength to hold your own in a room full of people who'd rather see you gone."
Drake snorted. "My mom would have loved this place. She always wanted to see the inside of a dwarf stronghold."
"She'd be proud," Cassian said, and for a moment the words hung between them, warm and dangerous.
Drake looked up. There was something in Cassian's eyes, a flicker of light behind the dark, but he couldn't name it. Maybe he didn't want to.
Lyra was already curled up in a mound of furs, snoring gently, wings twitching as she dreamed. Elliana had stationed herself by the door, knife drawn, but her head drooped as the liquor took effect.
Drake leaned back, staring at the ceiling. He let the mountain claim him, just for a little while, and dreamed of fire and stone.

Dawn came without sunlight. Instead, a chorus of anvils tolled through the Western Heart, vibrating the floorboards and rattling the crockery. Drake woke with a start, flinching at the racket, Lyra a tangle of hair and complaint, Cassian already halfway dressed, and Elliana, of course, ready and waiting by the door as if she had been up for hours.
"They're expecting us," Elliana said, tone dry as parchment. "Let's try not to get into any trouble before breakfast."
A page arrived, not a child but a dwarf scarcely taller than Lyra, clad in tunic and mail so heavy it could crush a lesser being. The page regarded them in silence, then gestured for them to follow.

The route to the Heart Chamber was different than the night before, winding through side corridors and up a lift that was more a suspended cage than an elevator. At each turn, dwarves paused their labor to stare—some openly, some through narrow glances, but all with the same wary intensity. Drake felt the scrutiny burning through him.

The Heart Chamber made the audience hall look like a broom closet. It was a perfect circle, hundreds of feet across, the floor stepped in tiers that rose to the walls, each tier packed with dwarves in formal dress—chain and scale and the occasional silk, all in colors Drake didn't know metal could hold. At the center, a ring-shaped forge pit blazed with a blue white flame, the heat so intense it rendered everything in wavering mirage. Around the forge were seven stone platforms, equidistant, each one carved with the sigil of a clan: mountain peaks, crossed hammers, gem-studded axes, an anvil bleeding molten gold.

On the dais of the Ironspine, Vorgat was resplendent: beard freshly braided and set with bands of platinum, armor polished to a mirror sheen. The other clan leaders were no less imposing.
