There was a woman with scars crossing her cheeks like claw marks, her armor chased with ice-blue enamel; a dwarf so old he seemed to predate the stone itself, eyes buried behind folds of wrinkled flesh, beard in a coil at his feet; a pair of twins in gold-plate, their motions mirrored down to the twitch of an eyebrow.
Lyra's wings quivered at the sight. "If anyone throws somethin', duck," she whispered.
"Don't give them ideas," Cassian murmured back.
The page led them down a wide, sloping aisle—past rows of silent onlookers—
and halted just shy of the inner ring, within spitting distance of the forge.

Elliana stepped forward, arms raised, voice booming: "Esteemed Clans of the forge born, we present ourselves by the ancient right of hospitality. We come in peace, seeking only to share our cause and make humble petition before your wisdom."
A ripple of approval—muted but present—moved through the audience. Vorgat rapped the pommel of his axe against his dais, calling order.
"Let the petitioners speak," he said.
Elliana nodded to Drake. He took a breath, feeling the dry burn in his throat. Every word mattered, he knew; every word was a chisel against the stone.

He addressed the dais, not just Vorgat but the whole assembly. "My name is Drake, son of Vivianne, half Drakkyn. I was sent to find the Soul Anchor, as the prophecy commands, not for power or profit, but to keep the realms from shattering."

He could feel the room grow colder—or maybe that was just nerves. "There's a darkness moving. Not just in Awen, but in the world above. We have reason to believe that the Soul Anchor, along with it’s counterparts, is the only thing that can bind the Veil and keep the two worlds from breaking apart."
The old dwarf with the glacial beard leaned in, voice like a cave-in: "Prophecy. Every week some fool claims it. Why should we listen to you?"
Drake swallowed. "Because I don't want the Anchor for myself. None of us do. We're just trying to stop something bad from happening to everyone."
The twins muttered to each other, then spoke as one: "And what will you do with it if you succeed?"
"Return it," Cassian said, stepping forward. "Seal it away. We're scholars, not conquerors. If you have the means to protect it, we'll leave it in your hands."
The council seemed to like that answer, or at least found it novel.
Vorgat gestured to Cassian. "You. Prove your words."

Cassian nodded, then stepped to the edge of the forge. He knelt, not in supplication, but with the focused intensity of a man communing with an ancient text. He laid a palm on the cold, black stone of the hearth, a gesture that was both reverent and proprietary.
"As I say, I am a scholar," he said, his voice carrying over the low rumble of the forge. "My magic is not to command, but to understand."

He closed his eyes and whispered a single word, a sound that seemed to draw the very essence of the mountain into the forge's heart. A ghostly, shimmering vision rose from the forge, not of the past, but of a terrible future. The dwarves saw their mountain homes crumbling to dust, their intricate carvings dissolving like sand in a storm. They felt the heat of their forges die, and their hammers rust into nothingness. It was a silent, terrifying prophecy of what would happen if the worlds were to break, a future where all their history and all their work was erased.
Cassian opened his eyes, and the vision vanished. He stood, his gaze sweeping the now-silent council.
"This is our fate if we fail," he said, his voice a quiet command. "We seek harmony. If the worlds break, this—the very stone and fire that define you—will be nothing but dust."
Lyra went next, at Elliana's prompting. She stepped forward, her voice a delicate, haunting melody that seemed to fill the cavernous chamber.

"I am a stranger here," she began, her gaze as clear as winter starlight. "But I know the feel of a world that holds its breath. My people—the Fae—we live on a razor's edge. Our world exists, but only because we constantly remember the song that keeps the balance. We know that a single wrong note, a single forgetting, could unravel everything we hold dear. I dinnae want to ask you to believe me. I ask you to believe in the balance you have here, and to fear what happens if you forget its melody."
A clan leader with a gem-studded helm nodded, slow and grave. "The fae speak truth. The world is not a forge; you cannot keep hitting it and expect it to stay whole."
Drake was surprised at how seriously they took Lyra; maybe, he thought, the dwarves knew what it meant to watch something beautiful die.
Elliana was last. She offered no speech, just a deep bow that was more a gesture of respect than of submission. When she straightened, her gaze was steady, meeting Vorgat’s with unflinching honesty.

“By the contract of the old realms,” she said, her voice clear and resonant, “we ask for your trust, not your judgment. The fate of our worlds is in peril, and we cannot save them alone. We promise, by the honor of my people and the word of my allies, that we will take the Anchor and use it only to restore the balance. Once the task is done, it will be sealed away, untouched by us forever. We ask you to trust that our intentions are true.”
Vorgat grunted, then gestured to a figure standing at the perimeter of the forge

—a dwarf unlike any Drake had seen before. The High Smith was silent, ancient, his arms sleeved in burn scars, his beard a dirty white rope trailing the ground. He carried a mythrilline hammer in one hand, its surface unblemished, the handle wrapped in strips of dragon-hide.

The High Smith approached, moving with the slow, inexorable dignity of a landslide. He regarded each member of the party in turn, then produced from his pocket a set of small, unremarkable metal bars—one gold, one iron, one lead, one unknown to Drake, almost black.

He set the bars on the anvil and, with a silent gesture, pointed to Drake. "A smith knows his metal by its ring," he said, his voice a whisper that commanded silence. "And I will know your soul by the sound it makes."

The High Smith picked up the iron bar. He held it to Drake's chest, then struck it once with his hammer. The impact rang out, a clear and pure note that seemed to echo through Drake's very bones. The High Smith nodded, a flicker of satisfaction in his eyes.

Next was Cassian. The High Smith picked up the lead bar, and as he held it to Cassian's chest, the metal seemed to absorb the light around it, becoming duller still. The hammer fell, and the sound was different—not a ring, but a low thud, a note of grim resolve. The High Smith nodded, his face unreadable.

Lyra went next. The High Smith picked up the black bar, and as he held it to her, the metal began to shimmer with an inner light, a faint, crystalline blue. The hammer struck, and the sound was a delicate, almost silent chime, like a silver bell ringing in a far-off place. The High Smith's gaze was ancient and knowing as he nodded.

Elliana was last. The High Smith picked up the gold bar. As he held it to her, the metal began to glow, radiating a soft, fierce heat. When the hammer struck, the sound was so sharp it hurt Drake's teeth. The bar vibrated with a furious energy, then settled into a single, resonant hum. The High Smith's face broke into a rare smile, and he gave a curt, respectful nod.
The High Smith collected the bars, tucked them away, and returned to Vorgat. He whispered something in the chief's ear, then gestured to a hulking dwarf who stood in the shadows near the great forge.
Vorgat nodded, then addressed the hall: "The council will now deliberate."
It was not a quick process. The seven clan leaders leaned in, voices low but heated. Hands gestured, axes thumped the dais. At one point, the twins seemed ready to duel, but cooler heads prevailed.
Finally, Vorgat stood. He lifted his axe and pounded it once into the stone. The other clan leaders did the same, one by one, until the chamber was full of the sound.

"It is the decision of the Western Heart," Vorgat proclaimed, "that your worth is not as you claim, but as you are. The High Smith has heard your hearts. You must now meet the Soul Smiths and pass the Trial of the Forge. Only then are you worthy to touch the Anchor."
"We accept," Drake said, hoping he meant it.

The council rose as one, and the hall erupted into a flurry of activity. Pages dashed off, runners barked orders, and the blue flames of the central forge intensified, sending up sparks that fell like fireworks.
As the party was led away, Lyra muttered, "What exactly is the Trial of the Forge, then, and who are these soul smiths?"
Cassian's smile was thin and sharp. "I have absolutely no idea... Sounds fun."

ch.src: Sebastian Nightwell and Thaddeus Johnson, Heart of the Drakkyn (2025), Chapter 24
p: The entrance to the Trial of the Forge was a wound cut into the living rock, framed in iron with dwarven runes hammered in relief so deep you could have lost a knuckle in any given glyph. The effect was equal parts intimidating and ceremonial; They were past the point of retreat—the doors had boomed shut behind them, the sound of locking bars like the closing of a tomb.

A Soul Smith awaited them just inside, broad as a wood stove and nearly as hot, sparks flicking from the exposed edges of his gauntlets as if he’d just come from the forge. The dwarf’s beard was braided to a point and capped with a slug of lead; his gaze skipped over Elliana and Lyra, then settled on Drake with a butcher’s precision.

“Four.” The Soul Smith made it a statement, not a question. “You go in together, you come out together, or not at all.” He spat to the side, where it hissed against stone. “Trial accepts no half measures. Prove your worth through fire, stone, and spirit.” He eyed Cassian, who was already squinting at the runes etched above the arch. “You like reading? Good. Sometimes reading is the only thing keeps your head attached.”

Lyra snorted, hugging her arms tight to her chest, but the blue glow of the ore veins in the wall washed the color from her skin until she looked nearly spectral, wings flickering with agitation. Cassian said nothing, just nodded once and kept reading, his lips moving as he worked over the syllables.
The Soul Smith thumped a fist to his heart, spun on his heel, and left. The sound of his boots faded in three strides, and then it was just the four of them and the yawning dark.

They walked. At first the tunnel was simple, just a corridor with walls arched and buttressed in that strange way only dwarves could manage—weight distributed so elegantly, even the hairline cracks felt calculated. But soon the walls began to twist, subtle at first, then with a more deliberate menace: passages funneled narrower, the ceiling lowered, the air staled and thickened until every breath was a taste of mineral and age.

Light was never absent, but never comforting. The veins of blue-green ore spidered through the stone, sometimes branching overhead in perfect fractals, sometimes pulsing faintly as if they were arteries feeding the mountain’s heart. In some places, the veins were so dense that the walls appeared to be stitched together by light alone, every other inch a constellation.

Elliana slowed at the first sign of something out of pattern. She dropped to a crouch, eyes flicking, and motioned for Drake to stop. Ahead, the tunnel widened into a short gallery, its floor a checkerboard of raised plates—none more than an inch higher or lower than the rest, but enough that a careless step would change your center of gravity.
“Trap,” she said, though it was probably obvious to everyone. “Pressure triggers, maybe.” She scanned the ceiling. “Drill axes, or something worse. Dwarves don’t bother with nets.”
Cassian murmured, “They write warnings, though. Look.”

He pointed to the lintel above the entrance to the gallery, where a fresh band of runes—different from the ones at the entrance, finer, less ceremonial—had been etched with a craftsman’s hand. Cassian leaned in, fingers hovering over the grooves.
“It says, more or less: ‘Only fools and cowards seek the quick path. Wisdom treads softly.’” He shot Elliana a glance. “So, probably don’t just sprint.”

Lyra sidled up to the edge, peering down the length of the gallery. “Think we could fly over it?” She stretched her wings, then recoiled at the touch of cold air. “Maybe not. Updraft’s garbage in here.”

Elliana began to probe the plates, toes pressing just enough to gauge resistance. The first few did nothing, but a quarter of the way in, she hit one that depressed with an audible click. Instantly, three rows ahead, a slot in the wall snapped open and a spinning drill bit the size of a thigh shot across the corridor, exactly head-height for a average human. It withdrew as quickly as it appeared, the air behind it reeking of singed metal.
Elliana grinned, not breaking stride. “Easy enough. The trick is to trigger them before you get there, then time the rhythm.”
Drake swallowed, sweat beading despite the cold. He did not like puzzles. He especially did not like puzzles that could unscrew his head if he guessed wrong.
Cassian stayed close, whispering the runes’ meanings as they advanced—

sometimes warnings, sometimes instructions, but always precise. Lyra hung back, waiting for the signal, but when Elliana tripped a plate and the next set of drill axes fired, Lyra darted across the open space with fairy speed, dodging the kill zone entirely.
“Show off,” Elliana muttered, but it was a compliment.

Two-thirds of the way through, Elliana misjudged. She pressed a plate, and instead of the expected drill whine, the entire floor lurched. The plates rearranged, sections collapsing, new ridges rising in a wave that almost knocked her sideways. She tried to backpedal but caught the edge of a new gap

—and would have fallen, but Lyra, already across, whipped a length of braided vine from her pack and flung it back, looping Elliana’s wrist. With a jerk, Lyra pulled her clear, the two of them ending in a pile on the far side.
Drake froze, paralyzed by the idea of falling. Cassian laid a steadying hand on his arm.
“Step exactly where I step,” Cassian said. “Don’t deviate.”

They crossed in tandem, Cassian moving with the careful, almost preternatural balance of a chess grandmaster. He read the plates, the runes, the patterns of shifting stone as if they were lines of poetry. Drake mimicked, muscle by muscle, and together they made it to the safe zone, where Lyra and Elliana waited, both breathless and grinning like idiots.
Past the gallery, the tunnel grew more hostile. The blue ore light was almost blinding in places, casting shadows that danced and crawled with every motion.

They encountered more traps: a section where the walls telescoped in, slow at first, then with a sick, hydraulic inevitability; a room filled with steam vents that hissed with such force the air shimmered and popped, each jet aimed just high enough to scald flesh from bone. In one corridor, the path was blocked by a tangle of glassy filaments stretched across the width—a web, almost invisible, that Lyra caught only by the faintest glint of reflected light.

“These’ll slice you to ribbons,” she said. “Best let me have a go.” She pulled a seed from her pouch, chewed it, and spat the pulp into her palm. Within seconds, a vine sprouted, pale and rubbery, its tip moving with a predatory slow intent. Lyra let it crawl ahead, using it to prod and snap the filaments, which parted with neat, wet slices.
“Never piss off a fairy,” Elliana said, deadpan. “They’re creative.”

All the while, Cassian grew more and more absorbed by the runes. He stopped frequently, tracing patterns with his fingers, sometimes scribbling notes in the dust or whispering translations under his breath.
“These aren’t just warnings,” he said, pausing before a particularly dense patch of script. “They’re… instructions. It’s like each set is tailored for whatever’s next.”
Drake eyed the next bend, where a stone arch bristled with glyphs. “Think you can read ahead? Save us some bruises?”
Cassian smiled, a rare crack in his otherwise reserved demeanor. “I can try.”

At the next challenge, they needed every bit of Cassian’s insight. The tunnel dead-ended at a door that shimmered with so much magical energy it left afterimages in Drake’s eyes. The door itself was a slab of slate, maybe a foot thick, its surface carved with interlocking rings of runes—each ring a different color, each rune a different texture, some raised, some recessed, some etched so fine you could barely feel them.
“Puzzle door,” Elliana said. “Classic.”
“Except,” Lyra pointed, “every time ye touch one, the whole pattern changes.”

Cassian stepped up, eyes narrowing. “It’s a sequence. Like a combination lock, but with syntax instead of numbers.” He pressed his fingertips to the outermost ring and waited. The runes pulsed, then rearranged, shifting inward. Cassian frowned, then tried another pattern, this time speaking the syllables aloud as he touched each symbol.

The door responded: the runes glowed in sequence, then clicked into a new alignment. Cassian kept going, sweat beading at his temples, every move more confident. Lyra and Elliana hung back, tense, watching for trouble.
Finally, Cassian spoke a word Drake had never heard, and the door’s entire surface went blank—then flashed once, painfully bright, and vanished. Not slid aside, not opened, just gone.

They stood at the threshold of something new. Beyond was another corridor, this one wider, lined with columns and murals showing dwarves working the forge, battling monsters, sometimes dying in droves, sometimes crowned in glory. The light here was softer.
Cassian exhaled, shoulders slumping in relief. “Next time,” he said, voice ragged, “I’d rather face a thousand drill axes than another linguistic puzzle.”

Drake clapped him on the shoulder. “You’re good at this,” he said, and meant it. He felt the fire in him, that Drakkyn stubbornness that wanted to solve every problem by force, quiet for once. Cassian had outsmarted the mountain, and for the first time, Drake wondered what else the scholar was capable of—what secrets he might unlock, given the time.

Elliana led them onward, but this time, Drake and Cassian walked side by side, their footsteps echoing in harmony. The Trial of the Forge was not over, but the party was stronger than when they entered, every trap survived another layer of trust forged between them.
They pressed forward into the blue-lit dark, ready for whatever the mountain would throw next.

The air changed when they hit the bridge. It was a subtle shift at first—a breath of heat at the backs of their throats, a glint of red layered beneath the blue luminescence of the ore veins—but the further they went, the more the temperature ratcheted up. By the time Elliana signaled a halt, sweat beaded on Drake’s forehead and rolled in sheets down the small of his back.

The bridge spanned a chasm so wide the far side seemed a trick of light, the intervening space blurred by an updraft that shimmered with all the colors of a welders’ torch. Below, a river of molten rock tumbled and seethed, surfacing in violent gouts wherever the ancient dwarven causeway shed a chunk of debris. Every hundred yards or so, a pillar of worked stone rose from the hellish current, carved with the same runes as the tunnel above. But here, the runes glowed blood-orange, and the heat pressed at them from all sides, a living thing eager to see what they would do next.
“This is madness,” Lyra muttered, squinting at the bridge. “If the tunnel wasn’t trying to kill us already, that lava’s got a personal vendetta.”
Elliana tested the first few paces, moving slow, then faster, then a full-out dash to the first landing. “Stable enough,” she called. “But don’t linger. The edges are
—” She never finished, because a shard of stone flaked off under her heel and spun into the abyss with a sound like a distant scream.

Drake, goaded by her bravado and by the certain knowledge that he could not let Cassian or Lyra go ahead without him, went next. The bridge flexed beneath his weight. He tried not to look down, but the light of the magma was hypnotic, a river of angry stars that beckoned with a promise of instant, annihilating peace.
Halfway across, the mountain groaned.

The sound was unlike anything Drake had ever heard. The supports of the bridge snapped, one after the other, sending a spray of pebbles skittering across the ancient paving stones. In the same instant, the ceiling above them began to crumble, slabs of granite the size of small cars tumbling down in slow, inevitable arcs.
“Run!” Elliana shouted, her voice muffled by the explosion of dust.
They ran.

For the first few paces, Drake was aware only of the heat and the noise, the way his lungs fought for air, the way his boots stuck to the lava-warmed stone. Then a slab crashed to his left, barely missing his shoulder. The concussion spun him sideways, right into Cassian, who caught him with a grunt.
“Keep moving!” Cassian yelled, but the world had slowed to a crawl. Each footfall felt like a minor act of rebellion, each breath a miracle.

A particularly massive rock broke loose from the ceiling, landed square on the bridge between them and the landing where Elliana and Lyra now waited. The stone lodged itself deep, splitting the bridge into two unstable sections. The far half, where Elliana and Lyra clung, wobbled but held. The near half—where Drake and Cassian stood—shuddered, tilted, and began to sag toward the lava river below.
“Shit,” Drake said. It was all he could manage.
Lyra reached for him, but the gap was already too wide. The chasm belched a plume of superheated air, and for a second, all four of them were separated by a wall of fire.

Cassian’s face was tight, his jaw clenched, but his hands were steady as he gripped Drake’s elbow and dragged him to the only high ground available—a stub of cracked stone, barely wider than a doorstep, but out of the direct line of falling debris.
For a heartbeat, there was silence. Then the bridge beneath them made a sound like tearing paper, and Drake’s stomach plummeted as the platform dipped even further.
“We have to jump,” Drake said, voice barely audible.
Cassian’s eyes—dark, unreadable, but flecked now with blue light from the magic gathering in his palms—met Drake’s. “We won’t make it. Not like this.”

A thin, bright pain spiked through Drake’s head. The heat, the panic, the smell of cooked stone—it was too much. His hands trembled, and his vision doubled, then tripled. He tried to focus on the far side, on Lyra’s desperate shout, on Elliana’s white-knuckled grip on the crumbling landing.
But mostly, he heard his own pulse, a roaring, angry drumbeat that filled every inch of his body.
Drake’s hands began to burn.

Not literally—not at first—but with a sensation of impossible heat, a pressure that threatened to tear the skin from his bones. He looked down, terrified, and saw that his palms glowed with a golden light, like embers trapped beneath the flesh. Panic took over, and the fire in his hands flared, licking up his wrists, wreathing his arms in a soft, flickering corona.
Cassian’s hand on his shoulder was ice in comparison. “Drake. Look at me.”
He did. And for a moment, the fire faded, beaten back by the calm, steady force of Cassian’s gaze.
“You’re not going to die here,” Cassian said. “We’re going to solve this. You just need to control it.”
“How?” Drake whispered. “I don’t—”
Cassian braced both hands on Drake’s shoulders, pinning him. “You’re Drakkyn. Fire is in your blood. The bridge is stone, not wood. It needs you. It wants you to fight.”
Drake stared at his hands, willing the fire to retreat. But the more he resisted, the hotter the pain became.

The next wave of debris crashed down, and Cassian threw up his left hand. Blue energy—pure, cold, focused—snapped from his fingers and formed a webbing of arcane force, holding the next chunk of ceiling in midair for a precious few seconds. The strain on Cassian’s face was visible, sweat beading on his brow, the veins in his neck standing out.
“I can’t hold this forever,” Cassian grunted.

Drake tried to think, but the panic threatened to swallow him again. The heat in his hands was worse now, molten, and when he reached out to touch the wall behind them, the stone blistered and then began to soften, running in slow, viscous beads away from his fingers.
“Use it!” Cassian shouted. “Melt us a way out!”

Drake didn’t think. He just pressed both hands to the wall, let the fire pour out, and watched in awe as the granite shuddered, turned glassy, and then sloughed away in a stream of magma. The smoke was brutal, but the new hole was real—
a tunnel, maybe big enough for two to squeeze through.

Drake dove in, burning away the rock as he went, not caring if his skin blistered or his hair singed. Cassian followed, maintaining the arcane shield around them, blocking the worst of the falling debris and the heat.
On the far side, Elliana and Lyra waited, battered but alive. Drake and Cassian burst from the wall in a spray of molten droplets and rolling steam, both of them gasping, sweat-soaked, and stunned.

The world was quiet again. The bridge behind them was gone, replaced by a mess of half-molten stone and a haze of sulfuric steam. Drake coughed, tried to stand, and nearly collapsed. Cassian steadied him, his hands gentle now, almost hesitant.
“Nice work,” Elliana said, but the smirk didn’t quite hide the relief on her face.
Lyra flitted over and stared at Drake’s arms, now raw but cooling, the fire already fading from the skin. “Ye look like hell,” she said. “But ye did it. Ye actually did it.”
Drake managed a laugh. “Never want to do it again.”

Cassian said nothing, but his hand lingered on Drake’s shoulder. It wasn’t just steadying; it was grounding, a touch that meant don’t run, don’t give in, I’m here. Drake leaned into it, just a little, and found he didn’t mind the closeness.
After a long moment, Elliana nudged them both. “Save the bonding for later. We’ve still got a trial to finish.”

The four pressed on, bruised but unbroken, Cassian and Drake walking in step, hands brushing together in the dark whenever the tunnel narrowed. The mountain had tried to kill them, but they’d carved a path through—fire and magic, together.

They reached the heart of the mountain by degrees, each corridor a narrowing spiral, each antechamber more oppressive than the last, until the air itself felt carved from the same unyielding stone as the walls. Yet even here, in the suffocating dark, the blue ore veins ran like lifeblood, illuminating their path with a glow that was almost gentle.

At last, the tunnel opened into a vast chamber, its floor a shallow dish polished to obsidian and ringed with pillars that soared up to a domed ceiling etched with constellations unknown to any of them. The stars above flickered with their own inner light, cold and white and impossibly remote. Drake paused, awestruck, and even Lyra, usually so quick with a quip, fell silent.
In the center of the vault stood a figure.

It was dwarven only in the broadest sense—nine feet from boot to brow, its form a lattice of enchanted steel, riveted stone, and bands of bronze as thick as Drake’s arm. Runes flowed across its surface in endless, shifting rivers, the teal light beneath animating the script so it seemed to swim, alive and angry, over every inch of armor. In both hands, the construct gripped a war hammer, the head the size of a full-grown mastiff, the shaft wound with links of something that gleamed like mercury.

The automaton’s head swiveled as they entered, and the eyes—just two blue points in a mask of iron—focused first on Elliana, then on each of the party in turn. When it spoke, the sound was a grinding, ancient thing.
“Those who seek the Soul Anchor,” it intoned, “must forge unity in conflict. Prove your mettle, or turn back. No other way.”
The hammer lifted, and the room shook.

Elliana was the first to move. She launched forward, knives flashing, rolling low and to the left—a feint, drawing the construct’s attention away from the others. The guardian was fast, but not as fast as a woman born to dance through traps; its first swing slammed down where she’d been a split second before, the impact sending a shockwave through the floor that nearly toppled Lyra.
“Don’t stand still!” Elliana shouted, already circling. “The vibrations are a weapon!”

Lyra responded by hopping between pillars, taking cover behind one before sending a handful of tiny seeds skittering across the stone. In seconds, the seeds sprouted, their roots writhing through cracks and seams, reaching for the automaton’s feet. The construct paid them no mind, until the roots coiled tight and yanked, tilting it just off-balance.
“Hit the joints!” Lyra yelled, wings fanned, sweat gleaming on her brow.

Cassian hung back, hands dancing as he conjured streams of blue fire—arcane bolts, tight and precise, that he sent whistling toward the guardian’s exposed gaps. The first few sizzled harmlessly off the armor, but Cassian adapted, aiming for spots where the runes were brightest, where the metal shimmered thin.
“Drake! When the runes pulse—those are the weak points!” Cassian called.

Drake had spent a lifetime learning to control his strength and his anger, to be careful in a world that punished excess. Now, with the taste of fire still raw in his mouth and the memory of molten stone behind him, he felt something break free. He sprinted toward the construct, keeping low as Captan Lyon had taught him, timing his approach to the guardian’s slow, inevitable turns.

The automaton caught sight of him and pivoted, the war hammer arcing with such force the air shrieked. Drake slid under the blow, fire racing along his arms, and punched both palms into the thing’s knee.

The metal didn’t just dent—it glowed, softened, ran in rivulets of red-gold. The construct staggered, off-kilter, and Elliana was there in an instant, her daggers flashing into the seam and twisting hard. Sparks erupted, followed by a spray of blue oil that steamed where it hit the floor.
Lyra’s vines worked their way higher, coiling up the guardian’s legs. She gritted her teeth, summoning another burst of growth, and the roots thickened, pulsing with green light.

The guardian roared, voice shaking loose dust from the ceiling. It jerked a leg free and brought the hammer down, aiming for Cassian this time. The young mage barely sidestepped, then raised both hands and fired a volley of blue-white bolts into the construct’s faceplate. The runes there flared, blinding, and for a moment the automaton staggered, confused.
“Now!” Cassian shouted, and Drake ran for it.

He leapt, the fire in him wild and impossible, grabbed the shaft of the war hammer with both hands. For an instant he felt the cold fury of the construct’s magic, an energy that wanted nothing more than to break him. But Drake held on, forced the fire out, and watched as the hammer’s head softened, sagged, then slumped off entirely and hit the floor with a hiss.

Elliana vaulted onto the guardian’s back, daggers digging into the base of its skull, prying at the seam. She wedged her blade in deep, then kicked off, landing hard but clear as the head plate popped loose.
The automaton lurched, staggering, and Lyra’s vines seized the moment, climbing into the gap and yanking back with all their might.
“Cassian!” Elliana shouted.

He stepped forward, eyes blazing. With a word and a gesture, he summoned a lance of blue light, sharper than anything Drake had ever seen. Cassian aimed for the exposed core, and the bolt struck true, burrowing deep into the construct’s heart.

The guardian froze, then convulsed, the blue light in its eyes going wild, sparking, then guttering out. It dropped to one knee, then the other, and finally crashed to the floor with a sound like the end of the world.
The silence that followed was total.
Drake panted, every muscle burning, but he was smiling. Cassian was already at his side, checking for wounds, hands lingering on Drake’s arms, his face open with a relief that bordered on joy.
“That was incredible,” Cassian whispered, but before Drake could answer, the ground beneath them rumbled, and a section of wall behind the fallen automaton slid away, revealing a chamber within.
Inside, on a plinth of obsidian, rested the Soul Anchor fragment.

It was not what Drake expected. He had pictured something heavy, solid—a staff, or a giant blade, or a gem. Instead, it was a lump of black metal, blunt and thick as a brick, that pulsed with a soft, ghostly light, the same color as the veins that ran through the mountain. As Drake reached for it, the air shimmered with a sudden, impossible cold.

He lifted the fragment. It was lighter than air, but the instant his skin made contact, a chilling, potent awareness settled in his mind. It was a silent, crushing knowledge of every soul bound to the mountain's stone. The air didn't stir, and the runes on the walls didn't glow. Instead, they seemed to go completely still, their shadows hardening into something solid, ancient, and permanent. Drake understood, then, why the Scythe was so precious.

It was not a weapon. The fragment in his hand was a burden of knowledge, a map, and a tomb. He could see the tunnels now, not as stone and earth, but as a vast, tangled weave of souls—the ancient ones who had died in the mountain, the miners who had fallen, the forgotten heroes and the nameless dead.
He turned to the others, his face pale.
Elliana was the first to break the spell, her voice a low whisper. "What is it, Drake? What do you see?"
Drake shook his head, blinking back the sudden tears that stung his eyes. "The mountain... it's a graveyard."
Lyra’s smile was gone, her wings shivering with a cold dread. "Is it planin’ tae kill us then?" she whispered.
Cassian touched the fragment, his fingers careful, reverent. He glanced at Drake, and their eyes met. "You are carrying the weight of a world now, my friend," Cassian said, his voice grave.

The ghostly images of the dead stirred in Drake’s vision, their silent faces turning to him as if waiting for a command. The shadows of the runes on the walls began to twist, forming a new path in the stone—one that spiraled up the dome, then through a gap none of them had seen before.
"Looks like it wants us to take the scenic route," Elliana said, and there was no anticipation in her voice now, only a weary resolve.

They followed the new path, the fragment guiding them through a series of hidden corridors that wound ever upward. Drake could feel the mountain’s dead watching them. He did not fear them, but the responsibility of their silent witness, that was something else entirely.

At last, after what seemed like days, they emerged into the open air. The cold was shocking, clean, slicing the sweat from their bodies in an instant. Behind them, the entrance to the mountain sealed, leaving only a faint outline in the stone.

They stood at the edge of the world, the mountain’s eastern flank dropping away into open plains, surrounded by mountains on one side, and the border of the fire lands to the other. Far in the distance, the sky was just beginning to lighten, the first hint of sunrise limning the clouds in gold.
Elliana stretched, popping her back. “One piece closer,” she said, her voice heavy with fatigue, “but at what cost?”
Lyra, her face serious now, wrapped her arms around herself for warmth. “Maybe we’re supposed tae find out.”

Drake and Cassian held each other’s gaze for a long, silent moment, the world falling away. In that quiet space between them, a grim acceptance bloomed that all of them, together, now carried the terrible weight of a hundred thousand dead.

ch.src: Sebastian Nightwell and Thaddeus Johnson, Heart of the Drakkyn (2025), Chapter 25
p: Jayke dreamed of home.

In his mind, he walked the familiar crystalline corridors of Frostspire Castle, trailing his fingers along walls that sang with a high, clear note when touched. The sound echoed through the vaulted chambers, a music that had been the backdrop to his childhood.
He breathed deeply, filling his lungs with the crisp scent of pine and winter herbs that wafted from the royal kitchens, where Chef Boreas would be preparing snowberry tarts and frost-flower tea.
The weight of his ceremonial cloak settled comfortably across his shoulders, its silver embroidery catching the light that streamed through ice-paned windows.
Home. Safe. Real.

But even as he reached for these comforts, the dream began to shift. The crystalline walls liquefied, running like tears down a face, reforming into cold metal. The singing ice became the mechanical buzz of equipment. The scent of pine twisted into antiseptic and electrical discharge. His cloak dissolved, replaced by the rough fabric of a prisoner's uniform.

The castle's Great Hall stretched and distorted, its elegant proportions warping into Verrin's laboratory. Twisted machinery sprouted from the floor like metal weeds, their surfaces etched with glowing runes that pulsed with sickly green light. And at the center of it all, a massive rift tore through reality itself—a wound in the world that leaked shadows and whispers.

Jayke tried to run, but his feet were rooted to the spot. The rift widened, hungry and insatiable. From its depths, Dr. Verrin emerged, his skin crawling with blue luminescent tendrils, his eyes no longer human.
"The bridge between worlds," Verrin said, reaching for him with fingers that stretched impossibly long. "You are the key."

Jayke jolted awake with a gasp that scraped his throat raw. The fluorescent lights flickered overhead, casting his reinforced cell in a harsh, unforgiving glow. His body ached with a bone-deep weariness that went beyond physical exhaustion. Yesterday's "session" with Dr. Vex had left him drained in ways he couldn't fully articulate—as if she had scraped his ice magic out of him like marrow from bone.

He tried to summon even a simple frost pattern, the kind he'd mastered as a child, but his power responded sluggishly, producing only a faint dusting of ice crystals that melted almost immediately in the cell's carefully regulated temperature. The effort sent spasms through his muscles and left a metallic taste in his mouth.

The containment runes etched into the metal walls pulsed with suppression energy. The pattern was hypnotic, designed to disrupt magical thinking and prevent concentration. Jayke had learned to look away from them, to focus instead on the small, concrete details of his prison: the exact dimensions of his cot, the number of steps from wall to wall, the precise timing of the guard rotations.

Days had passed since his initial capture—how many, he wasn't certain. Time blurred in this place, marked only by the sessions with Verrin and Vex, each one leaving him weaker than the last. But today, something felt different. The quality of silence had changed. He became aware of sounds he'd been too exhausted to notice before—a soft, rhythmic tapping from somewhere to his left, the rustle of feathers, a low keening that might have been singing or weeping.

Jayke pulled himself upright, ignoring the protest of his aching body, and approached the transparent front wall of his cell. For the first time since his capture, he truly studied the containment wing in its entirety, with clearer eyes than his first terrified observations.

The facility stretched before him, a landscape of cells arranged in a semicircle around a central monitoring station. Each enclosure was tailored to its occupant—some larger, some reinforced with additional wards, some modified with environmental controls. The overall effect was that of a grotesque museum, with living exhibits on display.

Directly across from him, the griffin he'd noticed upon arrival huddled in the far corner of a undersized cage, its once-majestic wings now hanging even more limply at its sides. When it raised its head, its golden eyes held something worse than the fear he'd first seen—resignation. The proud creature was losing hope with each passing day.

To his right, the dryad slumped against the wall of her glass enclosure, her barklike skin now more severely cracked, weeping sap that pooled at her feet. The single withering plant at the center of her cell had lost more leaves, its stem bending under an invisible weight. As Jayke watched, she reached toward it with trembling fingers, and the plant seemed to strain toward her touch, though neither could quite reach the other.

In a smaller cell nearby, the gnome sat cross-legged on the floor, his skin paler than Jayke remembered, mottled from too long without sunlight, eyes blackened from abuse. The walls around him were covered in scratch marks—
not random, Jayke realized now, but organized in patterns. Tallies, perhaps, or some kind of record.
And these were just the ones he could see clearly. Other cells held shadows and movements— the other beings whose forms he couldn't quite make out shifted restlessly in their confinement.
"Still taking inventory, Your Highness?" a voice drawled from the cell to his left.

Jayke turned to see the vampire watching him with sardonic amusement. Thorne—that was his name, Jayke recalled from their brief introduction a couple days ago. The vampire was leaner than before, his elegant features sharpened by hunger, the grayish cast to his skin more pronounced—the result, Jayke knew, of whatever the Order was using to suppress his vampiric abilities.
"They've increased the extraction parameters," Jayke said, not a question.

Thorne's smile was bitter, showing the tips of fangs that had been filed down even further since Jayke had last noticed them. "Very observant. Yes, our gracious hosts have been quite... enthusiastic with their harvesting lately. Something has them excited." He tilted his head, studying Jayke with eyes that held centuries of cynicism. "You've been their favorite subject, though. Special treatment for royalty."
Before Jayke could respond, a nervous voice called from his right. "They're coming. Morning check."

In the cell on that side, Mira pressed herself against the far wall, her features shifting more violently than they had during their first meeting—now her ears elongated to points, now her fingers extended into claws, now her eyes widened and rounded like an owl's. The changes were more erratic, rippling across her form in waves that matched her obvious distress.
"Breathe, Mira," Thorne said, his tone surprisingly gentle. "In for four, hold for four, out for four. Like we practiced."
The shape-shifter nodded, following his instructions, and her features stabilized somewhat, though her hands remained clawed.

A moment later, two guards in the Order's white uniforms marched through the containment wing, their boots clicking on the polished floor. They moved with the efficiency of people performing a routine task, barely glancing at the cells as they passed. One carried a tablet, making occasional notes. The other's hand rested on a weapon at his hip—not a gun, Jayke noted, but some kind of specialized energy device.

As they passed Jayke's cell, the guard with the tablet paused, studying him with clinical interest. "Subject 23 shows improved recovery rate," he noted aloud. "Increase extraction parameters by twelve percent for this afternoon's session."
Jayke met his gaze steadily, refusing to show the fear that coiled in his stomach. A Frostspire must never show weakness. His father's words echoed in his memory, a mantra he clung to even now.

The guards moved on, completing their circuit and disappearing through a heavy door at the far end of the wing. As soon as they were gone, the containment area filled with sound—sighs of relief, muttered curses, the griffin clawed once at the floor of its cage.
And then, clear and deliberate, the tapping resumed.
"The code has changed since you got back," Thorne said, noticing Jayke's attention on the sound. "Grimble—the gnome—updates it regularly in case they're listening."
"I've been too... distracted to learn it," Jayke admitted.

"It's a simple substitution cipher now," Mira explained, her voice steadier now that the guards were gone. "One tap for A, two for B, and so on. Most of us have adapted." Her form had settled into something mostly human, though her eyes remained unnaturally large and reflective.
"They're asking about you," Thorne added, head tilted as he listened to the tapping. "Wondering if you've recovered enough to join the conversation."
Jayke hesitated, then moved to the wall he shared with the gnome's cell. After a moment's consideration, he tapped once, then twice, then once again—"yes" in the simplest form he could manage.

The response was immediate—a flurry of taps that he couldn't fully decipher, followed by a wave of whispers and movement throughout the containment wing. The dryad straightened slightly, her cracked bark creaking. The will-o'-
wisp brightened momentarily. Even the griffin raised its head, eyes fixing on Jayke with renewed interest.
"Well," Thorne said dryly, "you've certainly made an impression. They think you might be our ticket out of here."
"Why would they think that?" Jayke asked.
Mira's expression was painfully hopeful. "Because you're important. Someone will come for you. Your family, your guards—they won't just leave you here."

The words struck Jayke like a physical blow. He turned away, unwilling to let them see the doubt in his eyes. Would his family come? His father had always put duty to the realm above all else. And with the Order's growing power, would the Council of Awen risk open conflict to rescue one prince?
He didn't know. And that uncertainty was almost worse than the certainty of abandonment.
To distract himself, he asked, "Has anyone new been brought in since I left?"
"No," Thorne said with a shrug. "But three have been taken. The jellyfish hasn't returned from its last session. Neither has the sprite from the far corner, or the salamander elemental."

From across the way, Grimble called out, his voice weaker than Jayke remembered. "Ninety seven days since my capture. sixty-three prisoners have come through in that time. thirty-two never returned from their 'sessions.'" He gestured to the scratch marks on his walls. "I keep the records."
"Willow is getting worse," Mira added in a hushed voice, nodding toward the dryad. "Her plant is nearly gone. When it dies..."
She didn't finish the sentence. She didn't need to. They all understood the symbiotic relationship between dryad and plant—when one perished, the other followed.
"And what have you learned about these 'sessions' since I've been here?" Jayke asked, though he already knew the answer from his own experience.
Thorne's laugh was bitter. "They're refining their technique. Each extraction takes more, leaves less behind. They've developed a new apparatus—more efficient, they say. More thorough."
The gnome nodded grimly. "I listen. Learn. The guards talk when they think we can't hear. They're excited about something. A breakthrough. The rift is stabilizing."
The rift from his nightmare flashed in Jayke's mind—a wound in reality, leaking shadows and whispers. He shuddered.
"But why?" Mira asked, her form shifting slightly as her agitation grew. "What do they want with Awen?"
"Power," Thorne said simply. "Isn't that always what humans want? More power than they know how to handle."

The conversation faded as each prisoner retreated into their own thoughts. Jayke returned to his cot, lying back and staring at the ceiling. Despite the dire circumstances, a strange calm had settled over him. He wasn't alone. And where there were others, there was possibility.
As he drifted in and out of uneasy sleep, memories surfaced—fragments of his childhood in Frostspire Castle, moments that seemed impossibly distant now.

He was seven years old, standing in his bedroom, face screwed up in concentration as he tried to create the perfect frost pattern. Not just any pattern, but his father's signature snowflake—an intricate design with six-fold symmetry and delicate, branching arms. The Ice King used it as his personal seal, stamping it into official documents and treaties.
"Again," Jayke muttered to himself, dissolving his latest attempt with a wave of his hand. "Focus on the center first, then build outward."

He extended his palm, summoning his power. The air above his hand shimmered, then crystallized, forming a perfect hexagonal core. Slowly, carefully, he extended the pattern, adding layer upon layer of intricate detail. His tongue poked out between his teeth as he worked, adding the final flourishes—tiny ice spirals at each tip, the mark of the Frostspire line.

When it was done, he stepped back, admiring his creation. It hovered in the air, catching the light, sending rainbow refractions dancing across the walls. Perfect. His father would be impressed. Would finally see that Jayke was worthy of his attention, his pride.

But when the appointed time came for their meeting, a royal messenger arrived instead. "His Majesty sends his regrets," the servant intoned, not meeting Jayke's eyes. "Urgent Council business requires his attention. Perhaps tomorrow."
Perhaps tomorrow. The same words he'd heard yesterday, and the day before.

After the messenger left, Jayke stared at his perfect snowflake, still hovering where he'd created it. Then, with a gesture more violent than necessary, he shattered it, sending ice shards scattering across the floor. In a final act of rebellion, he froze his father's favorite inkwell solid, knowing it would take hours to thaw properly.
A small victory, but it was all he had.
The memory faded as Jayke drifted deeper into sleep, only to be replaced by another—his father's hand on his shoulder, the only physical affection he could remember receiving from the Ice King.
"A Frostspire must never show weakness," his father said, voice stern but not unkind. "Our people look to us for strength. For certainty. We cannot afford to falter."
Jayke had nodded, straightening his spine, determined to make his father proud. To be worthy of the Frostspire name.

Now, in the confines of his cell, that memory felt like both burden and comfort. He was a Frostspire. He would not falter. He would find a way out of this place, not just for himself, but for all the prisoners trapped here.

Over the next several days, Jayke worked to strengthen his bonds with his fellow captives. Though they had exchanged brief introductions upon his arrival, now he sought deeper connections, sharing stories of Awen with anyone who would listen—descriptions of the crystalline spires of Frostspire Castle, the eternal twilight of the Eldrin Woods, the majesty of the elemental palaces. For many of the prisoners, especially those from Earth who had never seen Awen, these tales were like water to parched soil.
In return, they shared more of their own stories. Mira elaborated on her capture

—she had been living on the fringes of the city, part of a small community of shifters who kept to themselves. The Order had come in the night, with specialized nets and suppression devices. She alone had escaped the initial raid, only to be caught days later when she returned to look for survivors.

Thorne, initially reluctant to share more than surface details, eventually revealed deeper wounds—he had been present at the signing of the first treaties between supernatural beings and humans. "I believed in coexistence then," he admitted one night, voice low to avoid the guards. "Foolish optimism. Humans always fear what they don't understand, and fear leads to this." He gestured at their prison with a bitter smile.

Even the other creatures began to communicate more openly. Stormwing, the griffin, tapped out more complex messages with his beak, sharing tales of the mountain eyries where his kind once ruled. Nia, the will-o'-wisp, communicated through increasingly elaborate patterns of light that Mira translated for the others. And late one night, when the guards were absent and the lights dimmed to simulate night, Jayke woke to find Willow the dryad weeping silently, her tears nourishing the dying plant in her cell—a moment of beauty and resistance in their sterile prison.

Most valuable was Grimble, who continued his systematic collection of information. "They're accelerating their timeline," he reported after eavesdropping on a conversation between two scientists. "Something about 'convergence' and 'optimal conditions.' They're planning something big, and soon."

As they shared information, a plan began to form. Jayke had noticed that the suppression runes on their cell walls pulsed in regular intervals, weakening slightly at predictable times. If they could combine their powers during one of these weaker pulses, they might create enough magical interference to shortcircuit the wards.
"If we time it right," he explained to the others, "we might be able to break through. Not just one cell, but all of them."

"We tried something similar when you first arrived," Grimble reminded him, tapping out the history of failed escape attempts on his wall. "The Order learns from each attempt, makes the wards stronger."
"And we're weaker now," Thorne pointed out, his usual cynicism in full force. "They've drained more of our power since then."
"Maybe that's an advantage," Jayke countered. "They might have lowered their guard, thinking we're too depleted to try again."

The plan took shape: Jayke's frost magic, Thorne's shadow manipulation, and Mira's transformation would create the initial surge. Willow would contribute what remained of her plant energy, Nia would intensify her light to the maximum, and the other prisoners would add whatever they could. Grimble would count down, ensuring perfect timing.
Their attempt came during the night shift, when the guard presence was minimal. As the runes reached their weakest point in the cycle, Grimble tapped out the signal: three quick beats, then silence.

Jayke summoned every bit of frost magic he could muster, focusing it into a concentrated beam aimed at the weakest point in his cell's ward field. Across the way, Thorne's shadows writhed and twisted, probing the seams of his containment. Mira's form blurred, cycling through a dozen different shapes in rapid succession, each one pushing against the wards in a different way.

The combined energy made the air shimmer, the runes flickering as the system struggled to compensate. For a brief, glorious moment, Jayke felt the wards weaken, saw the transparent barrier of his cell ripple like water. Freedom seemed just a breath away.
Then, with a surge of power that made the lights throughout the facility flicker, the system stabilized. The wards snapped back into place, stronger than before, and alarms began to wail.
"Containment breach attempt in Sector 7," a mechanical voice announced. "Security protocols engaged."

Jayke slumped against the wall, exhaustion washing over him. The others looked equally defeated—Mira curled into a ball in the corner of her cell, Thorne's expression darker than ever, Willow's plant drooping further as if sharing her despair.
Within minutes, Dr. Vex stormed into the containment area, flanked by armed guards. Her lab coat blended in against the pristine white walls, but her yellow eyes gleamed with sadistic pleasure.

"How disappointing," she said, her voice carrying clearly through the wing. "And here I thought we were developing a understanding." She moved to a control panel at the central monitoring station, fingers dancing across the interface. "Cooperation would make this so much easier. For all of us."
With a few taps, she adjusted settings, and the temperature in the cells began to rise. Not dramatically at first, but steadily, inexorably.
"A small reminder," Vex continued, making notes on her tablet as she observed their reactions, "of who controls your environment. Your comfort. Your very existence."

The heat was particularly brutal for Jayke, whose elemental nature was attuned to cold. He curled into himself, trying to regulate his body temperature, but the effort drained what little magical reserves he had left. Across the way, Willow's plant withered visibly, its last leaves curling and blackening. Stormwing's feathers became brittle in the heat, several breaking off when he shifted position. Ember's light dimmed dangerously, flickering on the edge of extinction.

"Fascinating responses," Vex murmured, recording observations. "Subject 23 shows particular sensitivity to temperature fluctuations. Note potential for targeted environmental manipulation in future sessions."

She left them like that, suffering in their personalized hells, the guards stationed at the entrance to ensure no further escape attempts. Hours passed, the heat relentless, preventing even the comfort of lying down.

In this extremity, isolated in his misery, Jayke faced a moment of crisis. Doubt crept in, insidious and poisonous. What if he couldn't escape? What if his father never came? What if his magic continued to weaken until there was nothing left but an empty shell, another failed experiment in the Order's ledger?
A Frostspire must never show weakness. The words felt hollow now, a child's mantra with no power against the reality of his situation.

Then, as he watched condensation form on the glass observation panel of his cell, something clicked. The water droplets gathered, ran together, formed patterns that reminded him of the snowflake he had created so long ago. Water. Moisture. Even here, in this controlled environment, it existed.
And where there was water, there was potential for ice.

Jayke straightened, a new idea forming. He had been trying to draw solely on his internal reserves, his innate frost magic. But what if he could draw power from ambient moisture instead? Not just the condensation, but the steam in the ventilation system, the humidity in the air, the very breath of the other prisoners.

He closed his eyes, extending his awareness beyond his body for the first time. It was different from his usual magic—not a summoning from within, but a calling from without. He felt the water molecules in the air, the way they vibrated with potential energy, waiting to be transformed.

Focusing intently, he reached for that potential, not forcing it but inviting it, channeling rather than commanding. The sensation was strange but exhilarating—not depleting his reserves but adding to them, like a river finding a new tributary.
His frost magic pulsed outward in a new way, subtle but profound. The ward field around his cell flickered, not dramatically but noticeably, the runes stuttering in their rhythm.
Across the way, Nia brightened, sensing the change. Grimble sat up straighter, eyes widening as he recognized what was happening. Even Willow raised her head, bark creaking as she straightened.

"I know how we can do it now," Jayke called softly to Thorne and Mira. "It's not about power—it's about source. We've been trying to break the wards from inside, but we need to disrupt them from outside."

He explained his discovery, watching understanding dawn on their faces. The guards, stationed at the entrance, paid no attention to their whispered conversation, assuming them too weakened by the punishment to attempt anything further...
They were wrong.

As the night shift changed, and the temperatures were finally stabilized , bringing a brief moment when attention was divided, Jayke nodded to Grimble, who tapped out a new signal—four quick beats, then two slow.

The prisoners responded as one. Jayke extended his awareness to the moisture throughout the facility, drawing it toward the ward fields. Thorne sent his shadows creeping along the seams where the wards met the floor, exploiting the smallest gaps. Mira shifted into a form with elongated fingers, reaching through the flickering barrier. Nia flared brilliantly, the light creating interference patterns in the ward fields. Stormwing beat his slowly mending wings, creating a current of air that carried Jayke's frost magic further than he could have reached alone.
The wards began to dim, more substantially than before. A guard glanced their way, frowning, but before he could raise the alarm, the entire system flickered and went dark.
For a heartbeat, silence reigned in the containment wing. Then Grimble let out a whoop of triumph, and chaos erupted.

Jayke lunged forward, his hands already forming ice daggers. Thorne's shadows billowed outward like smoke, obscuring the guards' vision. Mira was halfway through her cell door when the emergency systems engaged.

A secondary ward field—thinner but more resilient—snapped into place with a sound like breaking glass. Jayke's ice daggers shattered against it. Thorne's shadows were forced back, compressed into his cell once more. Mira howled in pain as the new barrier caught her mid-transformation, forcing her to retreat.
"Containment breach in Sector Seven!" A voice blared through the facility. "All personnel to emergency stations!"
The guards recovered quickly, their training taking over. One slammed her palm against a crystal set into the wall, and the backup wards strengthened, pulsing with angry red energy.
"That was closer than last time," Thorne muttered, his eyes still fixed on the place where his shadows had almost—almost—broken through.
Jayke nodded, breathing hard but with a fierce light in his eyes. "Did you feel it? The primary system went completely down."
"We just didn't account for the secondary failsafe," Mira added, flexing her fingers that still tingled from contact with the emergency barrier.
Nia's light had dimmed to a soft glow, but her voice was steady. "I saw how the patterns interacted with the ward field. I can target the weak points more precisely now."
Grimble, who had been watching from his cell with uncharacteristic silence, finally spoke. "They'll increase security after this. Change protocols."
"Let them," Jayke said, his voice low but carrying to each cell. "Now we know it's possible. We just need to be smarter. Faster."

The guards were approaching now, faces grim, shock batons at the ready. But as they passed each cell, they saw only docile prisoners, apparently resigned to their fate. They didn't notice the glances exchanged, the subtle nods, the silent communication of those who had tasted freedom—however briefly—and found it worth any risk.
The doctors would hear of this incident. Security would tighten. But for the first time since their capture, the prisoners had something more valuable than freedom itself: they had hope.

ch.src: Sebastian Nightwell and Thaddeus Johnson, Heart of the Drakkyn (2025), Chapter 26
p: The road from the Dwarven city cut through a vast open plain, then wound its way toward the first outlying blocks of Razkanyr City, where it immediately turned to sand. The contrast was unsettling. Unlike the veins of ore that fed the dwarven stronghold, these streets pulsed with the thrum of desert heat, the glare so pure it burned every color raw and new.

They reached the city wall an hour before dusk. The last stretch was uphill, a hundred ragged yards of silty, ankle-deep sand that sneaked into boots and lungs. Lyra, who had complained about the cold for days, now relished the sun’s relentless attention, letting her wings soak the light until they gleamed like brass windowpanes. She buzzed a foot or two above the rest, pretending it was for reconnaissance but really just enjoying the air.

Razkanyr’s walls were a proclamation. Five stories tall and built from blocks of sun-melted sandstone, each stone was fit to its neighbor so precisely that even spider silk would have trouble slipping through the seams. Hammered copper bells, set at intervals, rang in a constant, shifting harmony with the faintest breeze. Above it all, a crown of glyphs scrawled around the parapet in a steady loop—“Would you look at that, it’s a city-wide ward,” Cassian said, “It is very old magic indeed, something seems to be different though, as if it is layered somehow.”

The gates themselves were open, a triple archway wide enough for four ox carts to pass abreast. The party approached as a unit, Elliana at the front, Cassian at her left, Drake and Lyra side by side in the slipstream.

They were twenty paces out when the Sentinels stepped from the shimmering heat haze of the gate, appearing with a coordinated suddenness that was deeply unnerving. They were unnaturally tall and slender, moving with a predatory grace that was both elegant and fluid as a stalking cat. Their uniforms were minimalist and functional—slate-black sashes over fitted cuirasses, with subtle bands of iridescent blue at the joints. Masks covered their faces, sculpted to exaggerate feline cheekbones and narrow the eyes to slits. While their movements were distinctly animalistic, it was the tips of their furred, pointed ears, constantly flicking to catch every sound, that gave away their non-human lineage.

Elliana stopped instantly, hands up and away from her weapons. Drake followed suit, as did the others. The Sentinels fanned out, their leader advancing with a precision that said the conversation was over before it began.
“Hands,” the Sentinel captain’s voice was a low purr that vibrated directly in Drake’s chest. He complied without thinking, presenting his wrists palm-up.

The shackles were not metal, but bands of golden-white light conjured from slim sticks the Sentinels produced from their belts. As the light touched skin, it shimmered and tightened, warm but unyielding. Cassian was already analyzing the construct, nostrils flared as if tasting the magic in the air. Lyra whimpered as two Sentinels bracketed her, gently but firmly pinning her wings.
“Hey—” Drake started, but Elliana cut him off with a sharp shake of her head.
“Keep your mouth shut unless spoken to,” she muttered. “These are Bast’s finest.”
Drake’s breath caught. Bast? Like the goddess from Earth’s myths? He’d seen her statues in museums, but to hear her name spoken as a living ruler sent a jolt of shock through him.

The Sentinels marched them through the gate. Inside, the city did not so much open as unfurl. The first block was a riot of shadow and sun, the alleys tight and vertical. The sandstone was painted in broad washes of deep blue and ochre, and banners of spun glass ribboned overhead, rippling in the high, dry wind. The air was so thick with heat and light that Drake felt it pressing against his eyeballs, squeezing the last chill of the mountain from his bones.
The streets were not empty. People clustered in every available shade—

humans in loose caftans, dwarves hawking wares from shadowy doorways, the occasional fairy perched atop a merchant’s awning. As the party was paraded through the plaza, eyes followed them with open curiosity. In one alley, a child pointed at Cassian and whispered to her mother, “Is that one of the Scholars? The human?” Cassian stiffened slightly, but did not break stride.

The march continued, every turn bringing them closer to the city’s heart. At one point, the road split over a massive irrigation canal, its water so impossibly clear and cold it seemed to hum with its own magic. Lyra craned her neck, wings fluttering, but a Sentinel guard redirected her with a flick of the wrist that was both gentle and an absolute command.

The palace rose from the city like the prow of a golden ship, a sprawl of terraces and pavilions stacked with careless audacity. The outer wall was inlaid with obsidian and fire-glass, flanked by two three-story statues of the city’s patron, Bast. Her likeness was hyperreal and terrifying, muscles rippling beneath carved basalt, eyes set with plates of silver.

At the threshold, the Sentinels halted them and stripped away the shackles in a single, synchronized movement. The light bands faded, leaving no mark. The captain gestured for them to proceed. It was not a request.

The interior was a cool, sweet shock, smelling of gardenia and something wilder. The ceiling soared into a dome of stained glass, filtering the sun into columns of blue and gold. The floor was black stone, shot through with bands of mother-of-pearl that traced out a map of the city.

Within moments, a figure approached—impossibly tall, draped in a white-andgold robe, her skin a deep, polished brown. Her eyes glinted with vertical pupils, yellow as sulfur. She walked with a rolling, predatory grace.
She stopped a few feet away, her gaze lingering on Drake. “You are expected,” she purred. “Follow, please.”

She led them down a corridor and through a set of gold-leaf doors into the audience chamber. Here, the ceiling opened to the sky, and the floor was a mosaic of river stone and onyx. At the far end of the room sat a throne—a simple bench, really—but the woman who reclined there made the entire room seem to bow toward her.

Bast was not what Drake expected. She was human, or close to it, her features delicate but strong, her hair a mass of tightly coiled black ringlets shot through with gold thread. Her eyes were the same impossible yellow as her minister’s, but their gaze was softer, almost amused. She wore nothing but a shift of pale linen and a heavy gold necklace stamped with ancient hieroglyphs.
The minister stopped short of the dais and bowed low. The room went silent.
Bast smiled—slow, deliberate, the kind of smile that meant you already knew the punchline but were going to enjoy watching someone else struggle for it.
“You come from the Western Heart,” she said. “You carry wounds, and questions. And something more.”
Drake felt the heat rise in his cheeks. He glanced at Cassian, who nodded, and then stepped forward.
“We seek safe passage through Razkanyr,” Cassian said, his voice even. “We have business with the Dragonkin, and we mean no harm to your people.”

Bast lifted a finger, silencing him. “Everyone means no harm, until they do. That’s why I built my city the way I did. You see the bells?” She gestured, and Drake realized they were everywhere, dangling from rafters and woven into braids. “Every bell is a node in my network. When one rings out of turn, I know. When one falls silent, I know that, too. There is no secret in this city that I do not hear.”
She leaned forward. “So, let’s not waste time beating around bushes. You are not simple travelers. You are the prophecy incarnate. The Realm's Hope. Or so my spies tell me.”
Drake’s jaw dropped. Elliana tried to hide a smirk. Lyra looked ready to faint.
Bast looked at Drake, then at Cassian. “Which of you is the fire, and which the chain?”
Cassian answered first. “I am the Scholar. This is Drake, son of Vivianne. He is… the bloodline you’ve been watching for.”

Bast’s smile widened. “Good. Honesty is refreshing.” She stood, her body a study in contradiction: predatory and beautiful, soft but obviously dangerous. “You may stay the night. My guest house is yours. But tomorrow, you will answer my questions, and you will do so truthfully.”

She walked down the dais steps, closing the distance to Drake with a disconcerting, feline ease. When she stood before him, she reached out and brushed her fingertips along his jaw. Her touch was electric, not painful but deeply unsettling. “Your heart beats like a dragon’s,” she whispered. “Do not let it rule your tongue.”

With that, she turned and vanished through a side door, the minister at her heel. The Sentinels gestured for the party to follow them to a suite of rooms carved from living rock. Food and wine were laid out on low tables, and beds were made up with linens so soft Drake thought he’d never get up again.
For a while, the four of them just stood in silence, digesting the day’s events.
Then Lyra, never one to let a silence linger, said, “Well, I like her better than the dwarf. At least she doesnae want us dead. Yet.”
Elliana poured herself a glass of wine, then looked at Drake. “You did good, kid. She’s going to test you, but I don’t think she’ll break you.”
Drake shook his head. “I have no idea what I’m doing,” he said, and Cassian smiled.
“Welcome to the club,” Cassian said, raising his own glass. “We’re all just making it up as we go.”

The sun set over Razkanyr in a blaze of blue and orange, the glass panels in the city walls throwing wild shadows across the streets. From somewhere far above, the bells began to ring the evening hour, their tones threading through the stone and the air, weaving a net of sound around the palace and its secrets.
Drake lay back on his bed, closed his eyes, and tried to imagine what tomorrow would bring.
He did not have to imagine long...

Dawn brought Razkanyr to riotous life. The palace bells rang the hour before sunrise, their tones shivering through the guest suite’s thin crystal windows and pulling Drake from a sleep so deep it took him half a minute to remember where, and who, he was. He sat up, blinking away the dream’s residue—
something about flying, scales, and a voice that felt like his own, but older—
and found Cassian already awake, perched at the edge of the divan, shirtless and immersed in the notes he’d scribbled on a borrowed tablet.

Lyra was sprawled on a silk pillow under the window, her wings flared and twitching in REM, and Elliana was nowhere to be seen. Only a faint tang of Elliana’s coffee, bitter and rich, remained as evidence of her passing.

Drake rolled to his feet, toes curling into the cool marble, and crossed to Cassian. For a moment, he stood in silence, watching the way morning sunlight traced the lines of Cassian’s back, each muscle so precise it could have been chiseled by one of the dwarven forgemasters.
“You been up all night?” Drake asked, voice husky.

Cassian smiled, not looking up from his tablet. “I slept. But I was right about the runes we saw yesterday.” He gestured at the page, where he’d transcribed fragments of the palace’s ever-present script. “It is a surveillance system, and it’s more complex than I imagined. Every message, every significant magical signature, it all feeds back to the center.”
“Bast?” Drake guessed.
Cassian nodded. “Ultimately, yes. This city doesn’t just have eyes—it has a memory.”
A sharp knock at the door ended the conversation. Elliana poked her head in, her expression somewhere between warning and exasperation. “Showtime,” she said. “We’re expected.”

The party dressed quickly, Lyra grumbling as she peeled herself off the pillow. Drake washed his face in the marble basin, and then followed Cassian out into the hall, Elliana already leading the way with the posture of a woman who knew every exit.

The throne room was at the center of the palace, beneath the great glass dome. The sunlight was filtered and amplified, painting the obsidian floor in shifting bands of blue, gold, and violet. The floor was so highly polished it reflected a whole second world, mirrored and upside down.

Bast awaited them, reclined sideways on her obsidian throne. Today, she wore a sheath of gold silk, her limbs bare and burnished, every finger adorned with rings. Her black hair was piled high and set with a single, enormous peacock feather. At her feet, the tail of a long, spectral cat—made entirely of shifting shadow and blue fire—coiled and uncoiled, never still.

When the party entered, Bast did not rise. The magical pressure in the room intensified, a palpable weight that made it harder to breathe. She regarded them with a slow, predatory pleasure, as if deciding whether to eat them, hire them, or let them go.
“Approach,” she said, and her voice filled the room, a rolling purr that made Drake’s skin rise in gooseflesh.

They obeyed, crossing the slick floor until they stood at the foot of the dais. Bast watched them for a long moment, her eyes flicking from one face to the next. When she spoke again, the words came sharp and precise.
“We begin with the Drakkyn,” she said, and Drake felt the focus of the room shift to him like the sun through a magnifying glass.
“You carry the fire,” Bast said, “but not just the fire. I can see the other blood, too. You are… what is the word?” She looked at Cassian.
“Hybrid,” Cassian supplied, his voice steady despite the pressure in the room.
Bast nodded. “Yes. I like hybrids. They are proof the world still wants to change. Why do you seek the Scythe of Thanatos?”
Drake swallowed, his mouth dry. “To save our friends,” he said, the words coming out rougher than he’d intended. “And to stop the Order from breaking the world.”

The spectral cat’s tail lashed, sending a ripple through the air. “Saving your friends—noble. Saving the world—arrogant.” She leaned forward, elbows on her knees. “What if the world needs to break? What if it wants to be something new?”
Drake blinked. “I don’t think anyone wants what the Order is doing.”

A smile touched Bast’s lips. “Not now, perhaps. But later, when enough pain has accumulated, change always finds a way.” She turned her gaze to Cassian. “And you—are you the brains of this operation, or just the scribe?”
Cassian bowed slightly. “I’m here to learn, and to keep the peace. Nothing more.”

Bast laughed, low and musical. “The Scholar. You think learning is neutral, but it’s always dangerous.” She shifted her attention to Elliana. “You are not from here,” she said, her tone amused. “But you walk like you own every room you enter.”
Elliana offered a courtly bow. “I’m a professional. The world pays for confidence.”
“True.” Bast’s smile widened. “And what would you steal, if you could steal anything?”
Elliana did not hesitate. “Time.”
Bast clapped her hands, delighted. “Honest thief! I wish more people would answer that way.” She looked to Lyra. “And you, little fairy. What do you want?”
Lyra flared her wings and lifted her chin. “To see the Veil restored. To go home, maybe. Or to find out if ‘home’ is even a real thing.”
The feline queen grew suddenly somber. “It isn’t. But you are welcome to try.” The whip of blue fire at her feet settled, curling into a spiral, and Bast rose from the throne.

“You seek the Scythe of Thanatos. Many have died for less.” She circled them, slow, each step measured and calculated. “What will you do when you find it? Who decides who lives, who dies, who returns?”
Drake thought of Jayke in that glass cell, the hope flickering behind his eyes. “I don’t know,” he said. “But I’ll try to do better than the people who made these rules in the first place.”
The admission seemed to satisfy Bast. She nodded, and the magical pressure in the room lightened, allowing them all to breathe easier.

“Three days ago,” Bast said, “a company of Drakkyn crossed the eastern pass. They carried fire, but also something heavier—despair, maybe, or a secret. I let them go, because it amused me to watch the mountain panic. But I doubt they’re amused anymore.” She glanced at Drake. “If you want to find your kin, that’s where you should look.”
She drifted back to her throne, every movement languid and precise. “Dismissed,” she said, and then ignored them completely, as if the conversation had never happened.
Outside, the Sentinels reappeared, guiding them back through the halls and out to the palace gardens. The moment they were free of the throne room, Lyra let out a shaky laugh.
“Was it just me, or did it feel like she wanted to eat us?”
“She does,” Elliana said, smiling thin. “But only if we’re interesting enough.”
Drake let his breath out slow, then looked at Cassian. “Did you catch the runes above the dais?”
Cassian nodded. “They said ‘the one who brings the blade will break the world, or save it.’” His eyes met Drake’s, and for a heartbeat, everything else faded.
“You believe that?” Drake asked, quiet.
Cassian hesitated, then nodded. “I think you’re meant to try.”

The rest of the day passed in a blur. They gathered supplies, rested, and planned their route eastward.
